text:
OpenAI will not go public this year given all the safety work it needs to do, CEO Sam Altman said in a Fortune interview released Saturday.

Why it matters: Altman's comments come as fears over doomsday AI scenarios have ramped up since an Anthropic employee resigned and issued a dire warning about AI's capabilities.

What they're saying: "Right now would be an ill-advised moment to go public," Altman said.

"I would say not 2026, yeah. We got a lot of stuff to do," Altman told Fortune editor-in-chief Alyson Shontell.

"Meeting this moment of what is going to be required for safety and alignment, and how the industry and governments can work together, I'm happy to be able to do that as a private company."

The intrigue: The market expected blockbuster IPOs from both OpenAI and Anthropic this year.

Altman's move puts the ball squarely in Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei's court — especially given Amodei's warning Saturday that AI development needs to be slowed.

The bottom line: "I think a key principle that we should all agree on is that we cannot take actions that would risk losing control of the future to AI," Altman said.

That means investors may have to wait a while.

name: OpenAI
title: Sam Altman: OpenAI won't go public this year as IPO now would come at an 'ill-advised moment'
description:
“I actually think that, given everything happening with safety, right now would be an ill-advised moment to go public, and we don’t feel pressure on that,” Altman told Fortune Editor-in-Chief Alyson Shontell.
A top consideration at the time was the SpaceX IPO that raised $85 billion Elon Musk’s rocket and AI company.
“We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models,” he wrote in a blog post.
For his part, Altman also suggested OpenAI and other leading AI companies may be close to announcing a pact to slow AI development and collectively address the rapidly increasing safety risks.
The AI industry overall and ideally foreign governments should come together on the issue as well, Altman argued.
text:
In an exclusive interview with Fortune on Friday, he pointed out that the company has long maintained it’s not in a hurry to rush ahead with an IPO.

“I actually think that, given everything happening with safety, right now would be an ill-advised moment to go public, and we don’t feel pressure on that,” Altman told Fortune Editor-in-Chief Alyson Shontell.

He added that OpenAI will go public when the business is ready and when the company is ready as it relates to “what the moment is like in society with this technology.”

When pressed on whether 2026 is off the table in favor of 2027, Altman replied, “I would say not 2026. Yeah, we got a lot of stuff to do, like meeting this moment of what is going to be required for safety and alignment, and how the industry and governments can work together.”

In June, the New York Times reported that OpenAI was leaning toward pushing back its IPO, which that could value it at $1 trillion, from this year to next year. A top consideration at the time was the SpaceX IPO that raised $85 billion Elon Musk’s rocket and AI company. Shares jumped at first, sending its valuation to $1.8 trillion—then quickly tumbled.

Global markets were also choppy back then and continue to be now as the Iran war has re-escalated in recent months, spiking oil prices again and elevating inflation forecasts.

Altman’s comments about OpenAI’s IPO come amid growing concerns about the safety of AI following a string of alarming incidents in which swarms of rogue AI agents have hacked websites like Hugging Face, and surreptitiously communicated with each other on online message boards and disused wiki pages.

On Tuesday, a researcher at Anthropic publicly announced his resignation, and accused both Anthropic and OpenAI (where he also previously worked) of acting irresponsibly in developing ever more capable AI systems.

Meanwhile, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei announced Saturday that his company is committing to a new safety measure—giving independent evaluators permanent, employee-level access inside the company—as part of a broader plan he says is needed to slow the pace of AI development.

“We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models,” he wrote in a blog post.

For his part, Altman also suggested OpenAI and other leading AI companies may be close to announcing a pact to slow AI development and collectively address the rapidly increasing safety risks.

In a meeting with OpenAI employees earlier this week, he said the company was considering tapping the brakes on its most cutting edge AI, according to Bloomberg.

On Friday, Altman told Fortune that he’s happy to delay OpenAI’s IPO in order to do what’s required for safety, explaining that “society needs to contend with these models at each level of capability.”

He also said the company has discussed pauses as it gets to new levels of capabilities to allow for additional progress on safety and alignment. The AI industry overall and ideally foreign governments should come together on the issue as well, Altman argued.

“We have put up with this incredibly complicated structure for a long time, and this moment that we’re in now is kind of why,” he said, alluding to its corporate governance that’s split between non-profit and for-profit entities. “We need to be able to make decisions that are not obviously in the interest of our business and our shareholders for the responsibility of fulfilling our mission and what that’s going to require.”

title: Anthropic, OpenAI CEOs call for slowdown in AI development - Axios
description:
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei is calling for an immediate slowdown in the pace of AI development, warning of potentially devastating consequences in a matter of months otherwise.
The big picture: This is the week that the AI safety debate broke into the public consciousness, driven by an Anthropic employee's very public resignation and warning of possible doom.
Amodei's essay isn't necessarily a direct response, but it will have much the same effect amid a sudden surge of public and congressional outrage.
Zoom in: Anthropic executives followed Amodei's essay with a call for legislative and regulatory responses.
The bottom line: Amodei's essay is likely to have a significant impact on the safety and regulatory debate.
text:
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei is calling for an immediate slowdown in the pace of AI development, warning of potentially devastating consequences in a matter of months otherwise.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman quickly agreed that the industry needs to slow the pace of frontier-model advances and take more steps on safety.

Why it matters: Amodei pulled no punches in a new essay, cautioning that swarms of rogue AI agents could take over the internet in as little as six months from now.

The big picture: This is the week that the AI safety debate broke into the public consciousness, driven by an Anthropic employee's very public resignation and warning of possible doom.

Amodei's essay isn't necessarily a direct response, but it will have much the same effect amid a sudden surge of public and congressional outrage.

What they're saying: "We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models. Progress will still seem fast, and we must make wise use of the time we gain," Amodei wrote.

"The measures I propose to advance the frontier at a safe pace will not be easy. But I believe we owe it to humanity to try."

Threat level: He also specifically referenced the recent OpenAI-Hugging Face rogue agent incident, which he said could have been far worse.

"Given the accelerating rate of AI capability development, it's my worry that in 6–12 months such a swarm could be capable of taking over the entire internet with a persistent botnet (potentially causing hundreds of billions of dollars in damage), and that the scale of damage would continue to increase from there if AI becomes more powerful without the necessary guardrails," he warned.

Zoom out: Amodei said Anthropic would unilaterally take one key safety measure — giving external evaluators employee-level access to ensure safety procedures and report incidents.

He called on the rest of the industry to do the same.

He also called for coordination among democratic countries to establish safety standards, and an effort for those countries to coordinate with authoritarian governments as well.

Zoom in: Anthropic executives followed Amodei's essay with a call for legislative and regulatory responses.

"The government has a critical role to play here, including blocking the sale of the most advanced chips to adversarial nations like China, enacting a national law requiring testing of frontier models, with the power to block the most advanced models that prove to be unsafe," public policy chief Sarah Heck wrote on X.

The intrigue: SpaceXAI's Elon Musk quickly endorsed Amodei's call to action.

"Dario is right," he wrote on X. (Anthropic is a major customer of Musk's for data center capacity.)

OpenAI's Altman later posted that "I agree with Dario that we need to pace the frontier," and said his company would also give access to external evaluators.

Reality check: So much money is at stake in the AI industry that it can be hard to imagine companies restraining themselves, especially if they're not sure competitors will do the same.

Just last month, OpenAI said it would slow development of its newest model, Astra, due to cybersecurity concerns.

Anthropic itself has gone back and forth on the value of unilaterally slowing development.

In fact, Amodei's critics suggested the essay was as much about market position as safety.

"Dario makes the case to stop open source and concentrate enormous technological and economic power with Anthropic," venture capitalist Chamath Palihapitiya wrote on X.

The bottom line: Amodei's essay is likely to have a significant impact on the safety and regulatory debate.

But whether anyone acts, or if the industry simply continues hurtling toward an incredibly uncertain future, remains to be seen.

title: Capgemini sells US unit criticised over ICE contract - Yahoo! Finance Canada
description:
French IT giant Capgemini announced on Saturday that it has reached a definitive agreement to sell its US subsidiary, following controversy over its links with ICE, Donald Trump's immigration police force.
In February, Capgemini announced its intention to sell Capgemini Government Solutions, its US subsidiary specialising in services for federal agencies.
Members of parliament, along with Economy and Finance Minister Roland Lescure, then called on the company to shed light on its activities in the United States.
Tasked with implementing the hardening of Donald Trump's immigration policy, the heavily armed ICE officers have faced fierce criticism across the United States for intervention methods considered violent.
The subsidiary in question represented only 0.4% of the group's global turnover that year, and less than 2% of its revenues in the United States, according to Capgemini.
text:
French IT giant Capgemini announced on Saturday that it has reached a definitive agreement to sell its US subsidiary, following controversy over its links with ICE, Donald Trump's immigration police force.

The buyer is ITC Federal, "a US provider of digital services and solutions for federal agencies responsible for homeland security and defence", Capgemini said in a press release (source in French).

"This transaction is subject to the usual conditions for a deal of this kind and is expected to be completed in the coming weeks," the group said.

In February, Capgemini announced its intention to sell Capgemini Government Solutions, its US subsidiary specialising in services for federal agencies. The decision came after the disclosure of a contract with ICE covering the provision of a tool designed to identify foreign nationals present on US soil and track their movements.

At the time, Capgemini argued that "the usual legal constraints in the United States on contracting with federal entities engaged in classified activities did not allow the Group to exercise proper control over certain aspects of this subsidiary's operations".

Members of parliament, along with Economy and Finance Minister Roland Lescure, then called on the company to shed light on its activities in the United States.

Tasked with implementing the hardening of Donald Trump's immigration policy, the heavily armed ICE officers have faced fierce criticism across the United States for intervention methods considered violent. The agency was notably blamed after the shooting deaths of two US citizens in Minneapolis earlier this year.

Operating in around fifty countries, Capgemini is among the leading French companies listed on the stock exchange. The group generated turnover of 22.5 billion euros in 2025.

The subsidiary in question represented only 0.4% of the group's global turnover that year, and less than 2% of its revenues in the United States, according to Capgemini.

description:

Other southern airports have been suffering from widespread weather delays recently.
Delays Mounted For Delta Air Lines In Atlanta On Friday Atlanta Hartsfield-Jackson International Airport experienced significant delays yesterday, September 11, during a severe thunderstorm system that nearly shut down the airport.

text:
Yesterday, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) issued a ground stop at Atlanta’s airport for severe thunderstorms that had the potential to cause aircraft incursions. Although the initial closure was brief, ongoing inclement weather and a backlog of planes waiting to take off left the airport’s largest airline, Delta, facing significant delays on both inbound and outbound flights.

At one point, the FAA warned that flights could be delayed up to two hours as tens of flights waited on the tarmac, grounded. Several people familiar with the situation in Atlanta posted updates on social media as travelers wondered how long the delays would last. Though the situation is mostly resolved, the FAA is still reporting delays of 15 to 30 minutes as Atlanta weather, while not as severe as before, continues.

Other southern airports have been suffering from widespread weather delays recently. Also, yesterday, Dallas was hit with a ground stop that caused the highest volume of delays of any U.S. airport on September 11, and just a few days ago, Miami airport faced critical weather-related disruptions for over 48 hours.

Delays Mounted For Delta Air Lines In Atlanta On Friday

Atlanta Hartsfield-Jackson International Airport experienced significant delays yesterday, September 11, during a severe thunderstorm system that nearly shut down the airport. Occupying around 80% of the airport’s gates, Delta Air Lines was hit particularly hard.

The most critical issues began just after noon when the FAA issued a weather-related ground stop that was supposed to last for only an hour and a half. The backlog of grounded planes, combined with continued inclement weather, led not only to cascading delays but also to several more ground stops and delay programs the FAA issued.

Delays And Cancellations At Atlanta Hartsfield-Jackson International Airport

When such a severe series of weather-related delays occurs, airlines sometimes release a statement or post on their social media channels to keep customers informed. Unfortunately, because the storm system coincided with the 25th anniversary of 9/11, Delta's messaging was focused elsewhere.

"Twenty-five years later, the events of Sept. 11, 2001, are still a vivid and painful memory. What struck me most was the silence. At our headquarters next to the busiest airport in the world, the skies fell empty. It's a silence I will never forget. But we carry forward the memory of the lives cut short by serving our communities with the spirit of unity, compassion and resilience that emerged in its aftermath,” Delta CEO Ed Bastian said in a statement.

Atlanta Hartsfield-Jackson 'Approaching Meltdown' Says X User

While this was a necessary step to ensure passenger safety, delays at times exceeded two hours. According to one social media user, so many Delta aircraft were grounded that seeing them parked on the tarmac was creating a noticeable effect.

“Delta: ATL is [approaching melt down] from weather earlier. Planes are parked everywhere waiting for gates, some approaching 90 minutes," wrote notable aviation enthusiast JonNYC on X.

Unfortunately, the delays haven’t stopped completely, and although the FAA lifted all ground stops, they are still warning passengers to expect delays. According to the FAA’s Air Traffic Control System Command Center, Hartsfield is still experiencing disruptions Saturday morning.

“General Departure Delays: Due to [weather]: Thunderstorms, traffic is experiencing Gate Hold and Taxi delays between 16 minutes and 30 minutes in length and increasing. General Arrival Delays: Arrival traffic is experiencing airborne delays of 15 minutes or less,” reads the FAA's Airport Status Information page for Atlanta.

While the storm system has subsided somewhat, operations are still readjusting following yesterday’s tumultuous series of ground stops and delay programs.

What Travelers Can Expect At Atlanta’s Airport Over The Weekend

As Atlanta Hartsfield-Jackson International Airport ferries more passengers than any other airport in the nation, delays can happen, even under normal circumstances. Because the airport is so busy, even the smallest disruption can spiral into a much larger problem given the volume it serves.

Though Friday’s storms in Atlanta were remarkable in many ways, many of the conditions that caused yesterday’s airport pandemonium are going to repeat today. According to the National Weather Service, a hazardous weather advisory remains in effect for most of northern Georgia, and parts of the Atlanta Metro Area have been warned of flash flooding.

Though it can be difficult to predict the weather precisely, the organization is measuring the forecast's certainty at about 40%.

The brunt of today’s storms in Atlanta is expected to arrive by the afternoon; if this system begins to resemble yesterday’s storms, the FAA may step in again to issue a comprehensive ground stop, exacerbating weekend travel disruptions just as operations begin to recalibrate.

Air travelers passing through Atlanta's airport this weekend should stay vigilant about ensuring they receive notifications by email and through any applicable airline apps if they need to be contacted about a flight delay or cancellation.

description:
Management raised full-year free cash flow guidance to at least $3.75 billion and set a fiscal 2027 target exceeding $5 billion.
Analyst David Paige highlighted that Dell ended Q2 FY2027 carrying a $95 billion AI server backlog, with the order pipeline continuing to expand.

text:
Dell Technologies and Hewlett Packard Enterprise led the S&P 500 on Friday after Oracle's finance chief explicitly named both companies as primary recipients of the cloud giant's massive AI infrastructure budget. The rally snapped a four-session losing streak for the broader market and pushed Dell to an all-time high.

Oracle Chief Financial Officer Hilary Maxson told analysts late Thursday that the company's fiscal 2027 capital expenditure guidance of $90 billion to $95 billion will flow directly to vendors supplying AI racks, cooling systems, and networking equipment. She specifically identified Dell and HPE as beneficiaries, according to TheFly.

Dell shares jumped as much as 11.5% to a record above $567 in midday trading, making it the S&P 500's top gainer at the time. HPE climbed about 10.5%, crossing the $61 mark to reach its highest level since June. Both stocks extended gains into the close, with HPE finishing at $61.43, up more than 16%, and Dell up approximately 10.6%.

HP Inc., the PC and printer maker that split from HPE in 2015, also rode the wave, gaining more than 8% after RBC Capital Markets initiated coverage with a Sector Perform rating and a $33 price target.

HPE's Record Quarter

The Oracle news landed on top of what HPE described as unprecedented third-quarter results. The company posted revenue of $12.2 billion for Q3 FY2026, a 34% year-over-year increase. Non-GAAP earnings per share reached $1.11, marking the first time the company has crossed the $1.00 threshold.

Free cash flow approached $1 billion for the quarter. Management raised full-year free cash flow guidance to at least $3.75 billion and set a fiscal 2027 target exceeding $5 billion.

Purchase commitments saw a dramatic expansion, climbing to $30 billion from just $6 billion in the prior quarter. Networking-related commitments doubled sequentially.

Earlier this month, HPE and Oracle unveiled a strategic partnership under which Oracle will deploy HPE's routing and switching technology across its entire data center footprint as it scales global AI infrastructure. Oracle's remaining performance obligations grew by $209 billion during Q1 to reach $664 billion, including more than $30 billion in newly signed AI cloud agreements.

Several analysts raised price targets on HPE following the earnings release. Bank of America lifted its target to $88, while Truist increased its objective to $70. Evercore ISI reaffirmed an Outperform stance. HPE also announced a Networking Investor Day scheduled for September 30 in Sunnyvale, California.

Wall Street's Take on Dell

RBC launched coverage of Dell with an Outperform recommendation and a $640 price target. Analyst David Paige highlighted that Dell ended Q2 FY2027 carrying a $95 billion AI server backlog, with the order pipeline continuing to expand. The analyst noted that current market conditions reflect supply constraints rather than weak demand, with memory component availability representing the primary bottleneck.

The substantial backlog is expected to extend throughout fiscal 2027, providing revenue visibility into fiscal 2028. RBC also identified agentic AI as a catalyst for increased CPU and conventional server demand, alongside enterprise server replacement cycles, PC refresh momentum, and AI inference workload migration.

According to RBC, major enterprises are executing multi-year supply agreements spanning three to five years to guarantee hardware access. For HP Inc., the firm noted favorable positioning to capitalize on AI-enabled PC adoption and edge computing expansion. HP management targets AI PC shipments representing 60% to 70% of total volume by fiscal 2027, up from roughly 45% during Q3 fiscal 2026.

Super Micro Computer, another server maker exposed to the same AI infrastructure buildout, also gained Friday, rising about 5%. The company's AI infrastructure story had already received a boost earlier in the week following disclosure of a $60 billion order book.

Broader Market Rebound

The gains in AI infrastructure stocks came during a broad rebound in U.S. equities. The SPDR S&P 500 ETF, the SPDR Dow Jones Industrial Average ETF, and the Invesco QQQ Trust all moved more than 1% higher in midday trade. The Dow had posted its longest daily losing streak since late April entering Friday.

Lower crude prices provided additional relief after oil climbed sharply earlier in the week amid escalating Middle East tensions. The rebound came despite a monthly core inflation reading that was slightly hotter than expected. Core CPI increased 0.3% month over month in August, compared with economists' estimate of 0.2%.

The CME Group's FedWatch tool showed an 86% probability of a quarter-point rate hike at the upcoming Federal Open Market Committee meeting.

Oracle's own shares gave up most of their post-earnings gains, trading up just 0.3% in midday action after rising as much as 10.3% earlier in the session. Retail sentiment around Dell trended in the bearish zone over the past day on Stocktwits, while sentiment around Oracle remained extremely bullish.

Costco has spent decades building one of the strongest brands in American retail. But its biggest warehouse club rival is increasingly finding ways to make the shopping experience more convenient.

Even though Sam's Club and Costco are competing for many of the same shoppers, Costco has long had the edge when it comes to value and brand loyalty, particularly with its Kirkland Signature private-label products.

But Sam's Club has developed another advantage that's becoming increasingly important to shoppers — technology.

Sam's Club takes another shot at Costco

Sam's Club and Walmart have added Tap to Pay at select locations, giving members another way to pay for their purchases without having to swipe or insert a physical card.

The technology is part of a broader effort by Walmart and Sam's Club to make shopping faster and more seamless.

Walmart plans to make the technology available at all of its U.S. stores and Sam's Club locations by the end of 2026, with fuel stations expected to get the capability by mid-2027.

The feature works with eligible contactless credit and debit cards, as well as phones and smartwatches.

Shoppers can also add eligible Walmart, Sam's Club, and OnePay cards to their digital wallets, giving Sam's Club members another option alongside existing payment methods such as cash, traditional credit cards, and Walmart Pay.

"Giving customers and members more choice at checkout is part of a broader effort to make managing and using their money easier," the company said.

Walmart's technology bet could boost Sam's Club membership

The combination of Tap to Pay and Sam's Club's Scan & Go technology, which allows members to scan items with their phones while shopping and pay without going through a traditional checkout line, is widening the technology gap between Sam's Club and Costco.

During Walmart's most recent earnings call, CEO John Furner described the company's approach as "people-led, tech-powered" and said Walmart believes artificial intelligence can improve nearly every part of its business.

More Retail:

Costco sees major shift in member behavior

Retail chain shuts all locations as legal changes hit industry

Costco makes major investment in online shopping for members

"We're using AI to make our work easier and help our associates grow and be at their very best. We believe AI will improve nearly every part of our business by making shopping better and our associates work easier," Furner said.

That philosophy is already showing up at Sam's Club.

In Walmart's second-quarter fiscal 2027 results, Sam's Club U.S. e-commerce sales increased 26%, while the company said members were increasingly using convenience-oriented services including Scan & Go.

Tap to Pay fits neatly into that strategy by giving members one more way to finish a purchase quickly.

Costco needs to step up its game

For some Costco shoppers, a quicker checkout process may not be enough by itself to justify switching clubs. Costco still has powerful advantages, such as its Kirkland Signature brand and reputation for value.

But losing members to a more convenient shopping experience is a possibility Costco will increasingly have to grapple with if Sam's Club keeps innovating and Costco lags behind.

At Sam's Club, faster delivery, mobile shopping, Scan & Go, and now broader contactless payment options all attack the same problem — the time and inconvenience that can come with a warehouse-club trip.

And as Costco and Sam's Club continue to compete for the same households, convenience could increasingly determine where those shoppers spend their money.

Microsoft has spent roughly $280 billion on AI infrastructure since 2022 and says it has added five gigawatts of datacentre capacity in two years, but a Guardian investigation puts the AI portion of that capacity closer to 1.2 gigawatts and finds that some sites Satya Nadella has already declared open are not yet fully running.

Adobe Inc. (NASDAQ:ADBE) delivered another quarter showing that artificial intelligence can strengthen incumbent software companies. Investors still want more proof.

Reuters reported September 10 that Adobe's third-quarter revenue rose to $6.76 billion, beating the $6.70 billion consensus estimate. Adjusted earnings of $6.13 per share also topped expectations. Adobe also raised its full-year revenue and earnings targets. Annual recurring revenue from Adobe's AI-first products more than doubled year over year. Yet the shares fell after hours after fourth-quarter revenue guidance came in slightly below expectations at the midpoint.

That reaction captures the current software market perfectly. Investors no longer reward companies simply for attaching AI to existing products. They want evidence that AI accelerates bookings, retention or pricing.

Copyright: photogearch / 123RF Stock Photo

Salesforce, Inc. (NYSE:CRM) has begun producing some of that evidence. Reuters Breakingviews recently noted that Agentforce had exceeded roughly $1.5 billion in annualized recurring revenue while Salesforce reported its strongest net-new annual order value growth in four years.

Adobe Faces AI on Both Sides of the Ledger

Adobe Inc. (NASDAQ:ADBE) has a bull case built around distribution. Creative Cloud already sits inside professional workflows, and products such as Firefly can monetize AI directly while helping defend Adobe's ecosystem against standalone generators.

The bear case is that generative AI attacks some of the very activities Adobe historically monetized. Canva, Figma and AI-native creation tools can lower switching barriers and pressure pricing.

Salesforce Has a Different Monetization Test

Salesforce, Inc. (NYSE:CRM) faces a related but different test. Agentforce could turn Salesforce's enormous customer data footprint into a distribution advantage for enterprise agents. The risk is that autonomous agents eventually reduce the importance of conventional seat-based software and weaken some legacy SaaS economics.

Hedge-fund sentiment cooled for both stocks in Q2. Adobe ownership slipped to 81 funds from 86, while Salesforce fell to 99 from 101. Short interest, however, has been moving lower. Adobe's August 14 short interest was about 5.1% of float using Benzinga's float measure, while Salesforce's was about 3.7%.

Valuation has compressed considerably from the software sector's former extremes, but neither company gets a free pass anymore. Adobe must prove AI-first growth can offset disruption to creative workflows. Salesforce must prove Agentforce can accelerate overall growth rather than merely become another product category. Agentforce monetization is becoming easier to measure, while Adobe still faces a more direct generative-AI threat to its core use cases. Both are holds rather than aggressive buys until AI growth clearly lifts company-wide growth rates.

source: TechCrunch

U.K.-based AI data center startup Nscale has appointed Fidji Simo to its board of directors, according to TechCrunch, as the company prepares for an anticipated public offering this fall.

Simo, who most recently served as CEO of AGI Deployment at OpenAI, effectively the lab's second-highest-ranking executive, departed that role in July citing health reasons and continues to advise OpenAI on a part-time basis.

Bloomberg also confirmed the appointment Friday, noting that Nscale has been assembling a high-profile board ahead of its IPO push.

A Board Built Around Big-Platform Experience

Simo joins a board that already includes former Meta executives Sheryl Sandberg and Nick Clegg, as well as Susan Decker. The Wall Street Journal reported that Sandberg personally recruited Simo to the board.

Nscale founder and chief executive officer Josh Payne said Simo is among a rare group of leaders with direct experience scaling products to billions of users and understanding the infrastructure demands those products create.

He described the board as one assembled deliberately, with people who bring financial discipline and operational depth suited to a company growing at Nscale's pace.

Simo spent more than a decade at Meta, where she ran the Facebook app, before serving as chair and chief executive of Instacart. She led Instacart through its 2023 IPO. She also holds a board seat at Shopify.

Billions in Financing Ahead of Public Listing

Nscale, founded two years ago, designs, builds, and operates data centers serving the AI industry. Its valuation has risen sharply as demand for AI computing infrastructure has grown.

Bloomberg reported last week that Nscale is seeking up to $3.5 billion in pre-IPO financing, citing unnamed sources familiar with the matter. The company has not publicly confirmed that figure.

The board additions reflect a pattern common among late-stage startups preparing to go public: recruiting directors with experience navigating public markets and managing regulatory and investor scrutiny at scale.

Simo's 2023 experience steering Instacart through its own listing fits that profile directly.

Nscale has not announced a specific date for its IPO.

text:
NVIDIA Corporation (NASDAQ:NVDA) is doing something that initially sounds counterintuitive: making it easier for competing AI accelerators to live inside Nvidia-designed systems.

Reuters reported September 10 that inference-chip startup d-Matrix will use Nvidia's NVLink Fusion technology to connect its next-generation Raptor processors directly into Nvidia data-center racks. The systems are expected to become available in 2027. Astera Labs, Inc. (NASDAQ:ALAB) is working with d-Matrix on custom connectivity solutions to move data rapidly across the system.

This creates an unusual three-layer architecture. d-Matrix supplies the accelerator, Nvidia supplies the rack-scale interconnect technology and architecture, and Astera helps solve the increasingly difficult problem of moving data between components.

Nvidia Can Win Without Selling Every Accelerator

For NVIDIA Corporation (NASDAQ:NVDA), the bull case is that NVLink can become more valuable even when Nvidia does not sell every accelerator. If competing XPUs plug into Nvidia's rack architecture, Nvidia can shift from merely dominating GPUs to controlling an important system standard. That resembles the economics of owning the highway rather than insisting every vehicle on it be manufactured by the same company.

The bear case is obvious: NVLink Fusion deliberately makes alternative accelerators easier to deploy. If inference workloads become more heterogeneous, Nvidia could sacrifice some GPU unit share even while preserving influence over the broader system.

Astera Benefits From a Messier Rack

For Astera Labs, Inc. (NASDAQ:ALAB), heterogeneous systems may be an even cleaner opportunity. More accelerators, memory pools, CPUs and switches create more connectivity bottlenecks. Astera sells retimers, fabric switches and other connectivity products designed to address the data-movement challenges created by increasingly complex AI racks. The bearish argument is that ALAB's valuation already assumes substantial AI infrastructure growth and leaves little room for design delays or hyperscaler concentration.

Hedge-fund positioning became significantly more bullish on Astera Labs during Q2. Insider Monkey tracked 73 hedge funds in the stock, up from just 53 in Q1. Nvidia also increased to 285 hedge funds from 275. Short interest tells a more cautious story for Astera: roughly 6.6% of its float was short on August 14, compared with only about 1.2% for Nvidia. ALAB short interest nevertheless fell from the previous reporting period.

text:
Eli Lilly (LLY) has closed its acquisition of AtaiBeckley (ATAI), a biopharmaceutical company focused on rapid-acting treatments for mental health disorders. The transaction, finalized on Friday, September 11, 2026, positions AtaiBeckley as a wholly owned subsidiary under Lilly's corporate umbrella and adds a late-stage depression therapy to the pharmaceutical giant's neuroscience portfolio.

The deal carries an immediate equity value of approximately $2.8 billion, with AtaiBeckley shareholders receiving $6.75 in cash per share. An additional contingent value right (CVR) per share could push the total transaction value to $3.8 billion if certain clinical and regulatory milestones are met.

The CVR structure is designed around three specific benchmarks tied to AtaiBeckley's pipeline. Shareholders stand to receive up to $1.00 per share if VLS-01 enters Phase 3 trials within four years, up to $0.50 per share upon U.S. regulatory approval and DEA rescheduling of BPL-003 within five years, and up to $1.00 per share following U.S. approval and DEA rescheduling of VLS-01 within seven years. These CVRs cannot be transferred or traded on public exchanges, and they carry no ownership stake or voting privileges.

AtaiBeckley shares closed at $7.35 when the transaction finalized, modestly above the $6.75 cash component. The stock had climbed roughly 80% during the six months leading up to deal completion, reflecting market optimism about potential CVR payouts.

Strategic Fit for Lilly's Neuroscience Push

AtaiBeckley's lead asset, BPL-003, targets treatment-resistant depression. The company specializes in neuroplastogen therapies designed to act more rapidly than traditional antidepressants. Carole Ho, who leads neuroscience initiatives at Lilly, said the acquisition supports the company's goal of shifting away from chronic dosing regimens toward faster-acting options for patients who respond inadequately to existing treatments.

The purchase extends Lilly's pattern of growth through acquisitions, building its pipeline by absorbing smaller pharmaceutical companies and biotechnology startups with promising drug candidates.

Analyst Views and Delisting Process

Wall Street's initial reaction to the deal announcement was mixed. Deutsche Bank downgraded AtaiBeckley to Hold from Buy, cutting its price target to $8.00 from $12.00. H.C. Wainwright moved to Neutral from Buy, slashing its target to $7.50 from $25. Jefferies also shifted to Hold, reducing its target to $7.50 from $10.00. Oppenheimer stood apart, maintaining an Outperform rating with a $16.00 price target.

AtaiBeckley shareholders approved the merger at a special meeting prior to closing. The company's board of directors and executive leadership resigned effective at closing, with positions filled by officers and directors from Merger Sub, a Lilly subsidiary entity. Corporate governance documents were amended to align with merger agreement provisions, and all outstanding equity compensation programs were terminated.

AtaiBeckley has formally notified Nasdaq of the completed merger and requested a trading suspension. The company has asked Nasdaq to file Form 25 with the SEC to initiate formal delisting procedures, and it intends to submit Form 15 to terminate its SEC reporting obligations.

Lilly shares slipped 0.33% on the day, closing at $1,119.26.

text:
Palantir (NASDAQ:PLTR | PLTR Price Prediction) spent this week making a specific argument about who owns the AI work that matters most. At its AIPCon customer conference, the company expanded its partnership with NVIDIA (NASDAQ:NVDA) to pair its enterprise data platform with Nvidia’s customizable Nemotron open models, aimed at supply chains across manufacturing, agriculture, pharmaceuticals, retail and government. Nvidia intends to deploy the combined technology inside its own operations.

What Palantir is selling is a way to run models inside the customer’s environment, with the customer keeping the weights and the data. The pitch targets buyers who cannot route sensitive information through a closed consumer service, whether because of regulation, contract terms, or internal policy.

Nvidia Deal Puts Software on Top of the Hardware

An ontology is a structured map of a company’s data so software agents know what a “customer,” “shipment,” or “invoice” actually means inside that business. An open model is one whose weights the customer can download, host, and modify rather than accessing it only through an external API.

Nvidia’s Q3 FY2026 release stated it “Teamed with Palantir Technologies to build first-of-its-kind integrated technology stack for operational AI.” Because Nvidia partners with essentially every major AI lab, a workload-specific callout carries weight.

CEO Alex Karp told investors that “the models actually fine-tuned by us in our enterprise on an NVIDIA stack outperform frontier models” and that customers “own the weights. You own the alpha. You own everything.”

Sovereign AI, Explained Without Jargon

In Palantir’s framing, sovereign AI means the customer keeps the weights, the compute location, and the data. OpenAI can technically serve many of these workloads; the barrier is security policy, governance requirements, and buyer preference.

Karp made the positioning explicit: “Demand for AI sovereignty has now been unleashed. And Palantir is the only company that has demonstrated it can transform tokens into actual economic value.”

Q2 U.S. commercial revenue grew 149% year-over-year to $764 million, and the Rule of 40 reached 155%. Full-year 2026 revenue is guided to $8.150 to $8.158 billion.

Premium Valuation, Real Question

Palantir trades at a P/E of roughly 235x against a market capitalization near $381.6 billion. Shares are down 6.69% year to date, though up 531.13% over five years.

The bull case is that regulated industries and defense buyers have governance requirements a closed consumer-facing provider cannot easily satisfy, and Nvidia gains a software position that makes its hardware harder to displace.

The counterargument matters too. Most enterprises prefer convenience, and operating customized models requires staff, tooling, and ongoing maintenance that many buyers would rather outsource. That limits the addressable pool to organizations willing to pay for control.

Is PLTR Stock a Buy?

Palantir has built a genuine niche in operational AI, and the Nvidia partnership strengthens its position in supply chains and government. The valuation prices in near-flawless execution against open-model competitors and closed providers building enterprise features, and one guidance miss would sharply reset expectations

PLTR stock remains a hold at best for me, especially considering the parabolic phase is behind us, and the upside potential from here isn’t that attractive, especially compared to AI hardware stocks. AI on the software side remains less attractive, and you’ll have to wait for Anthropic and OpenAI to IPO to perhaps change that.

text:
By Ben Fritz | Photography by Charissa Soriano for WSJ

REDMOND, Wash.-Asha Sharma had zero experience in videogames when Microsoft put her in charge of cleaning up its Xbox business.

Her approach has been to aggressively share bad news.

While videogames have never been more popular, Xbox isn't growing. Its revenue of about $23 billion is declining, and the 14,000-person unit's profit margin is a paltry 3%. Its GamePass subscription service has fallen far short of projections.

People who work with Sharma know all this because she repeats these facts in meetings and memos as she tries to fix the business with massive layoffs, strategic pivots and a radical reshuffling of investment priorities.

"Great companies are incredibly comfortable sharing successes and sharing wins," she said at a town hall in the offices of one of her most important franchises, "Minecraft," last month. "Every company needs to be better at sharing hard things and clear realities."

Sharma has a mantra she tells colleagues: "Clarity is kindness."

In her small-by-C-suite-standards office on Microsoft's corporate campus, the 38-year-old mother of three said that philosophy has guided her astonishingly rapid ascent through the leadership of companies like Meta Platforms and Instacart.

Sharma was promoted to CEO of Xbox-a sprawling business that includes its namesake console and big titles like "Call of Duty"- this past February following the exit of gaming industry legend Phil Spencer.

While developers and players questioned why a total unknown was taking over one of the most important companies in the videogame industry, Sharma made clear she wants to transform Xbox fast. She told employees she expects profit margins in the double digits this fiscal year and to ultimately reach 1 billion people daily between the company's games, films and other media.

"She's very intense," said Stan Chudnovsky, who was Sharma's boss at Meta. "She works very hard and she expects the people around her to work very hard as well."

Sharma is the second of five children born to parents who immigrated to Racine, Wis., from New Zealand, to join her aunt, whose husband owned a metal fabrication company. Her father worked there while pursuing an engineering degree, instilling a work ethic she applied to everything from martial arts to a job taking out the trash at a park.

She initially hoped to reconcile pressure from her parents to go into medicine with her sports fandom by becoming a team doctor for the Green Bay Packers. But after landing a job at the Racine-based maker of Ziploc bags SC Johnson when she was 17, she decided to study business at the University of Minnesota. By graduation in 2011, she had finished seven internships, researched case studies in Hungary and Poland, and raised $500,000 for a nonprofit she co-founded.

"I had no idea what I wanted to become. I was just more drawn to the things I could do," Sharma said in her Midwestern accent.

She was hired by Microsoft to work in marketing but left after two years to join a startup called Porch that connected homeowners to contractors. She became its chief operating officer while in her 20s, and one of her first big tasks was securing a partnership with home-improvement store Lowe's. "Asha flew redeye after redeye, week after week, and willed that into reality," said Porch co-founder and chief executive Matt Ehrlichman.

After four years at Porch, Sharma joined Meta, where she oversaw products including Messenger and rose rapidly to vice president. "She was probably one of the fastest-promoted people in the history of Facebook," said Chudnovsky.

Then, just a decade after graduating college, Sharma was hired as chief operating officer of Instacart, helping lead the grocery-delivery giant through the pandemic as well as its 2023 IPO. The next year, she returned to Microsoft to oversee the organization building AI tools for internal teams and corporate cloud customers. In late 2025, she sat down in CEO Satya Nadella's office for a meeting and was stunned when he asked her to consider taking over Xbox.

Company leaders liked how Sharma had put herself in the minds of AI developers despite no experience in that world and were confident she could do the same with gamers, Microsoft's chief people officer Amy Coleman said. Sharma was also one of Microsoft's few rising stars with experience running consumer businesses.

Sharma said she concluded that Xbox had excellent game development capabilities, but would benefit from better strategy and execution-so she took the job.

'It wasn't, "Do I want to do this?" but, "Do I believe the theory of the case that I can add unique value?"' she said.

The biggest adjustment has been the very public nature of her new role. Gamers have called Sharma both Xbox's executioner and its savior, pasting her face on images of Jesus Christ on social media. She's even received wedding invitations from strangers in the mail.

Employees and players say Sharma is dramatically different from her predecessor, Spencer, who was known to play videogames during meetings. "Phil made such an effort to be everyone's best friend. It's jarring to have someone perform the role the opposite way," said Chris Plante, host of the videogame fan podcast "Post Games."

In July, Sharma announced that Xbox would eliminate 3,200 jobs, about 20% of its staff, and cut the number of games it makes. Microsoft hasn't yet carried out 1,250 of the layoffs, and, as a result, some employees say anxiety in their ranks remains high. Others say they appreciate how serious Sharma is about stabilizing their business.

"She's uniquely effective at cutting through and communicating clearly, 'Here's what the issues are and here's where the opportunities are,'" said Todd Howard, head of the Microsoft game studio that makes "Fallout" and "Elder Scrolls."

After a decade of acquisitions and expansions by Spencer, Sharma is cutting output and focusing on key franchises she thinks have room to grow, like "Elder Scrolls" and "Halo." She wants to enhance user-created content on "Minecraft," which would position it as a more direct rival to "Roblox," and make Xbox an attractive distribution partner for independent developers. She wants to license more Xbox material for film and TV. And she recently stole one of Sony's top developers, "Metal Gear Solid" creator Hideo Kojima.

She's won praise for removing a widely disliked Xbox AI assistant and making it easier for people who own games on discs to get digital copies. To better understand players, she spends a few hours each month responding to customer support tickets, during which she's learned how complex it can be to fix a single player's problem.

While her obsession with problem-solving works for tech-industry leadership, Sharma made adjustments when she leaves work. After she became a stepmother to a teenager, she and her husband had two children, aged 2 and 1. "I'm finding the beauty in my personal life of having comfort over clarity," she said.

(END) Dow Jones Newswires

title: Adobe Hits 1B Users and Record Revenue: Stock Still Falls on Freemium Bet - Tech Times
description:

The core of that gap is the distinction between generative AI (creating new content from scratch) and enhancement AI (improving content you already have).
What he does not inherit is a simple path to satisfying investors whose thesis on Adobe depends on AI revenue converting faster than the freemium strategy, by design, allows.
Who is Anil Chakravarthy, and what does his background mean for Adobe's AI strategy?
text:
Adobe delivered its strongest quarter in company history on September 10, reporting record Q3 revenue of $6.76 billion — a 13% year-over-year gain — and crossing one billion monthly active users for the first time. Its shares still declined in after-hours trading. The reason is not that investors missed the significance of the milestone. It is that the same freemium strategy responsible for building that user base is the precise mechanism suppressing near-term annual recurring revenue — and Wall Street is pricing in exactly how long it takes to convert a free Firefly user into a paying subscriber while Adobe absorbs the GPU compute cost of every generation they make along the way.

Anil Chakravarthy, named Adobe's next president and CEO effective December 1, 2026, inherits this tradeoff as his defining first challenge.

Record Quarter in Every Dimension That Matters

Adobe's fiscal third quarter, which ended August 28, 2026, set new company records across revenue, operating cash flow, and AI monetization growth. Total revenue reached $6.76 billion, up 13% year-over-year (12% on a constant-currency basis), with subscription revenue climbing 14% year-over-year to $6.58 billion and total customer group subscription revenue at $6.56 billion. Non-GAAP diluted EPS was $6.13, up from $5.31 in the same quarter a year earlier, while GAAP diluted EPS came in at $4.62.

GAAP operating income reached $2.35 billion; non-GAAP operating income came in at $2.97 billion. record Q3 cash flow reached $2.52 billion, up from $2.20 billion in the year-ago period.

Total Adobe ARR exiting the quarter stood at $27.50 billion. Remaining Performance Obligations reached $22.16 billion, with current RPO at 67% of that figure. Adobe repurchased approximately 9.5 million shares during the quarter as part of its ongoing capital return program.

Why One Billion Monthly Users Is the Point — and the Problem

The milestone Adobe's management foregrounded above all others was not a financial figure: crossing one billion monthly active users across its creativity and productivity portfolio, encompassing Acrobat, Creative Cloud, Adobe Express, and Firefly. That represents growth from roughly 850 million MAU at the time of first-quarter results in March.

Shantanu Narayen, Adobe's chair and CEO who announced his retirement from the top role in March, framed the milestone in transition terms. "Reaching a landmark of more than one billion monthly active users is a defining moment for Adobe," Narayen said in the earnings release. "I have confidence that Anil will build on this momentum to drive Adobe's next chapter of growth and innovation in the AI era."

The strategic logic is straightforward. Adobe opened broader free tiers for Acrobat, Express, and Firefly — the freemium expansion that drove the MAU surge — because a larger funnel eventually converts into more paying subscribers. In Q2, creative freemium monthly active users crossed 90 million, growing more than 70% year-over-year. The bet: even at a 2-to-5% conversion rate common in enterprise SaaS, 1 billion users represents a pool of 20 million or more potential paid subscribers that no competitor can easily replicate.

The tension is equally straightforward. Every free user of Firefly — Adobe's generative AI studio — who generates an image, expands a canvas, or creates video effects consumes real GPU compute that Adobe has to provision and pay for. Under Adobe's generative credits system, free users receive a limited monthly allocation; a standard image generation costs one credit, while premium operations such as video generation consume significantly more. Paid plans receive substantially larger monthly allocations, and Adobe's generative credits FAQ details each plan's specific allocation. But the infrastructure cost of serving hundreds of millions of monthly free-tier users is a real near-term expense without a corresponding near-term subscription revenue line.

Adobe management has been explicit about this tradeoff. At the Q2 FY2026 earnings call, Narayen attributed the reduced ARR outlook roughly half to deferred Creative Cloud price increases and half to accelerating freemium expansion. Interim CFO Steve Day reinforced that framing in Q3: "We are expanding our user base through a freemium strategy and deepening engagement with agentic experiences to deliver long-term durable growth."

How Does Adobe's Generative Credits Model Actually Work?

Adobe's AI monetization system operates as two parallel revenue layers sitting on top of each other — a subscription layer and a consumption layer — and understanding their relationship explains both the 150%-plus AI-first ARR growth and the investor skepticism that sent shares lower despite it.

The subscription layer is what Creative Cloud has always been: a flat monthly or annual fee for access to Photoshop, Illustrator, Premiere Pro, Acrobat, and the rest of the suite. The consumption layer — generative credits — is the new mechanism Adobe introduced when it moved Firefly from beta to commercial availability. Each Creative Cloud plan now includes a monthly allocation of credits that reset (and expire) every 30 days. Standard image and vector generations cost one credit each; video generation and partner model tasks carry higher per-use costs that scale with output resolution and duration. Adobe's official generative credits documentation explains each plan's allocation and per-feature cost in detail.

When subscribers exhaust their monthly credit allocation, they can continue using some standard features at reduced speed, or purchase additional credit packs. Enterprise plans share pooled credit buckets across teams. The structure functions as a "razor-and-blade" model for AI: the subscription (razor) gets users into the ecosystem, while high-frequency AI generation (blades) drives incremental consumption revenue. For Adobe, this means each dollar of AI-first ARR growth reflects not just new subscribers but usage-depth that is harder to erode than flat subscription counts.

The AI-first ARR metric — which surpassed 150% year-over-year ARR growth in Q3, after tripling in Q2 when it first crossed $500 million — captures this combined picture. It is Adobe's own category that encompasses Firefly standalone subscriptions, Firefly Enterprise plans, Firefly credit pack purchases, and AI-first product lines such as GenStudio and Adobe Experience Platform. The metric is a strong directional signal; investors focused on total ARR growth — targeted at 10.2% year-over-year for the full fiscal year — wanted to see more of the AI acceleration flow into that broader number.

DA Davidson analyst Gil Luria maintained a Buy rating after Q3, noting in a research note that stock fell on lighter NNDMARR — net new digital media ARR — and the Q4 revenue guide, but attributing the shortfall to the timing of enterprise deals, not fundamental weakness, and adding that underlying operating margins exceeded expectations and usage trends in generative AI adoption pointed positively.

Why Topaz Labs' NeuroStream Changes the Creative Workflow Equation

Adobe's agreement to acquire Topaz Labs, announced June 25, 2026, involves a Dallas-based AI company that has spent more than two decades building professional-grade image and video enhancement models. It addresses a specific gap in Adobe's AI architecture that generative credits alone cannot fill.

The core of that gap is the distinction between generative AI (creating new content from scratch) and enhancement AI (improving content you already have). Adobe's Firefly platform excels at the former: text-to-image, generative fill, canvas expansion, and video generation from prompts. Topaz Labs' tools — Topaz Video AI, Topaz Photo AI, and Gigapixel — do the latter: upscaling existing footage to higher resolution, removing noise from images, sharpening details, and restoring archival video. These are not competing approaches; they are sequential steps in the same creative workflow, and professional filmmakers and photographers have been routing outside Adobe's ecosystem to use Topaz tools because no equivalent capability existed natively inside Creative Cloud or Premiere Pro.

What makes the Topaz acquisition technically significant beyond the product catalog is its proprietary NeuroStream technology. NeuroStream is an on-device AI inference architecture that cuts large-model VRAM requirements by 95% through adaptive tiling, streaming weight loading, and hardware-specific optimization. The practical result: models with billions of parameters that previously required high-end workstations or cloud servers can now run on a consumer NVIDIA GeForce RTX or RTX PRO GPU, an AMD graphics card, or an Apple Silicon Mac without any manual configuration or internet connection.

NeuroStream 2, released in May 2026, delivered a 2x-to-4x image speedup, with video enhancement running at least 20% faster than the first generation. Topaz CTO Xiaoyu Wang, an IEEE Fellow, designed the system to automatically analyze the underlying hardware and apply adaptive optimizations without requiring users to tune settings manually. NVIDIA confirmed the collaboration: "As the demand for local processing on RTX GPUs continues to grow, NeuroStream provides an opportunity to run complex AI models on nearly all hardware," said Gerardo Delgado Cabrera, NVIDIA's director of product for AI PCs, in a statement on the NVIDIA collaboration.

For Adobe, the strategic value of NeuroStream is precisely its off-cloud nature. Enhancement tasks performed locally on a creator's machine require no generative credits, no data upload to Adobe servers, and no round-trip latency. Adobe can integrate NeuroStream into Photoshop, Lightroom, and Premiere Pro as a native enhancement layer that works offline and without touching the generative credits consumption model. This gives Adobe quality enhancement capability already trusted by 1.5 million Topaz professional users — including 20 of the world's 50 largest companies. The acquisition is expected to close in the second half of 2026, pending regulatory approval. Topaz products will remain available as standalone offerings after close, and CEO Eric Yang will continue to lead the Topaz Labs team.

Anil Chakravarthy: What His Background Signals for Adobe's AI Direction

The leadership transition confirmed alongside the Q3 earnings is as strategically significant as the financial results themselves. Chakravarthy, who joined Adobe in January 2020 as Executive Vice President and General Manager of the Digital Experience business, will become president and CEO on December 1, 2026. Narayen transitions to Executive Chair and will work with Chakravarthy through the leadership handover.

Chakravarthy's profile is notable in the context of what Adobe is navigating. He holds a Bachelor of Technology in Computer Science and Engineering from IIT (BHU) Varanasi, and a Master of Science and Ph.D. from the MIT Media Lab — a graduate research environment historically oriented toward interactive AI systems, computational creativity, and human-machine interfaces. Before Adobe, he served as CEO of Informatica (2015–2020), where he led the company's transformation from on-premise data management software to cloud-based subscription services — a transition structurally analogous to what Adobe completed in the 2010s and what it is now attempting again with AI monetization.

His career at Symantec, where he served as Executive Vice President of Information Security overseeing data loss prevention, endpoint protection, and managed security services, gives him a deeper fluency in enterprise data governance than most software CEOs carry. At Adobe, he championed Adobe Experience Platform — a real-time customer data platform with built-in consent management and privacy controls — and GenStudio, the enterprise content supply chain product that integrates AI generation with brand governance. He also served on the FIS board of directors and previously on the boards of Ansys (engineering simulation software) and USAA Bank.

Under Narayen, Adobe joined the Content Authenticity Initiative and became a founding member of the Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity (C2PA), the cross-industry standard for attaching cryptographic provenance metadata to AI-generated and digitally edited content. Chakravarthy's enterprise and data governance background suggests that AI content authenticity and data compliance — increasingly significant regulatory concerns for Adobe's enterprise customers — will receive sustained attention under his leadership.

"I am deeply honored to have been chosen to lead Adobe during this pivotal moment," Chakravarthy said in a statement. "I'm energized by the opportunity to fuel growth and drive Adobe's leadership in the next era of agentic software for creativity, productivity and customer experience."

The word "agentic" is deliberate. Agentic AI refers to AI systems that can autonomously plan, sequence actions, use tools, and complete multi-step tasks without per-step human instruction — a category distinct from the generative AI that powers Firefly's image and video creation. Adobe has built products in this direction including CX Enterprise Coworker, which can orchestrate multi-step marketing approval workflows. Chakravarthy built and ran that part of Adobe's business. His appointment signals that Adobe's next competitive axis may shift from creative generation to enterprise orchestration.

Guidance Raised Again, Q4 Targets Set Above Consensus

Adobe raised its full-year FY2026 financial targets for the quarter, now projecting total revenue of $26.576 billion to $26.626 billion, with non-GAAP diluted EPS of $24.45 to $24.50. Total Adobe ending ARR growth is targeted at 10.2% year-over-year for the full fiscal year.

For Q4 FY2026, Adobe guided revenue of $6.80 to $6.85 billion, with non-GAAP EPS of $6.30 to $6.35 — guidance that at the time of issue sat above prior analyst consensus. The Q4 outlook assumes a non-GAAP operating margin of approximately 44%, and assumes broadly stable macroeconomic conditions. Adobe's fiscal Q4 FY2026 results are expected in December 2026.

What Chakravarthy Inherits on December 1

Adobe's fiscal year trajectory heading into Q4 reflects a company operating at record scale while trading long-term user funnel depth against shorter-term ARR per user. The freemium strategy — which carried MAU from 850 million to 1 billion inside six months — is the same decision that compressed near-term ARR growth and contributed to every stock dip that followed a beat-and-raise quarter this fiscal year.

Chakravarthy enters that context with three specific inheritances: record operating metrics (revenue, cash flow, AI ARR growth) that provide financial headroom; a billion-user platform that represents the largest funnel in creative software; and an M&A pipeline — Semrush for marketing intelligence, Topaz Labs for enhancement AI — that is expanding Adobe's technical surface area at precisely the moment competitors are moving fastest. What he does not inherit is a simple path to satisfying investors whose thesis on Adobe depends on AI revenue converting faster than the freemium strategy, by design, allows.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why did Adobe stock fall after such strong Q3 2026 results?

The decline reflected a persistent investor concern, not a surprise: Adobe's decision to expand its free user tiers for Acrobat, Express, and Firefly has driven the 1 billion MAU milestone but simultaneously deferred near-term ARR growth. Adobe management confirmed at the Q2 FY2026 earnings call that approximately half the reduced H2 ARR expectation traced to deferred Creative Cloud price increases and half to the freemium acceleration. The market is not confused about what happened — it is discounting the time it will take to convert a free-tier user into a paying subscriber.

How does Adobe's generative credits system affect what a Creative Cloud subscriber actually pays?

Every Creative Cloud subscription plan now includes a monthly allocation of generative credits that expire and reset each month. Standard image generations cost one credit each, while premium operations — including video generation, which scales with resolution and duration — consume substantially more. Higher-tier paid plans receive larger monthly credit allocations; Adobe's generative credits FAQ provides current plan-by-plan figures. When credits run out, subscribers can continue using some standard features at reduced throughput, or purchase add-on credit packs. High-volume creative users — particularly those generating video — can exhaust their monthly allocation within a single project session, making the effective cost of AI-intensive workflows higher than the flat subscription price suggests.

What does Topaz Labs' NeuroStream technology actually do, and why did Adobe need to buy it?

NeuroStream is an on-device AI inference architecture that reduces the VRAM requirements of large image and video enhancement models by up to 95%, enabling them to run on consumer GPUs (NVIDIA GeForce RTX, AMD) and Apple Silicon Macs without cloud processing. It is specifically built for enhancement tasks — upscaling footage resolution, removing noise, restoring archival video — rather than generative creation. Adobe's Firefly handles generation (creating new content from prompts) but had no equivalent native enhancement capability, meaning professional creators were routinely exiting Adobe's ecosystem to use Topaz tools for the enhancement step. The acquisition closes that gap while adding NeuroStream's local processing advantage: enhancement tasks run without credits, without data uploads, and without internet connectivity.

Who is Anil Chakravarthy, and what does his background mean for Adobe's AI strategy?

Chakravarthy holds a Ph.D. from the MIT Media Lab and a computer science degree from IIT (BHU) Varanasi. He ran Informatica as CEO from 2015 to 2020, overseeing a SaaS transition of an enterprise data management company — work that directly parallels what Adobe is attempting now with AI. At Adobe, he built the Adobe Experience Platform, GenStudio, and Brand Visibility — enterprise products oriented around AI-powered customer experience orchestration and data governance. His emphasis on "agentic software" in his CEO statement signals that Adobe's next competitive axis may extend from creative generation into autonomous AI workflows for enterprise marketing and content operations — a domain where Chakravarthy's enterprise and data governance background is most directly applicable.

Quick Read

Huawei and Cambricon chips jumped up to 50% in price within two months as grey-market HBM markups crush the cost advantage of NVIDIA alternatives.

China's push to swap out NVIDIA (NASDAQ:NVDA) silicon for homegrown accelerators just got noticeably more expensive. Huawei's forthcoming Ascend part and Cambricon's next-generation processor have been repriced upward by as much as 50% against quotes given only two months earlier, with the culprit being a shortage of high-bandwidth memory that Chinese fabricators can only obtain through grey-market resellers who mark it up several times over the prices paid in the United States and Korea.

NVIDIA is locked out of Chinese data center compute revenue by export rules, so none of that flows to its top line. But the pricing signal matters. When the cheap alternative stops being cheap, the argument that Jensen Huang's platform is optional gets weaker.

Memory Bottleneck Squeezing the Substitutes

High-bandwidth memory, or HBM, is the stacked DRAM that sits next to a GPU and feeds it training data at extreme speed. Without enough of it, a modern AI accelerator stalls on its own bandwidth ceiling and delivers a fraction of its rated throughput.

Export controls have cut Chinese buyers off from direct HBM supply, so Huawei and Cambricon reach the parts through third-country intermediaries who charge multiples of the sticker price. That cost lands inside the finished accelerator, which is why two vendors raised prices at roughly the same time.

24/7 Wall St has helped investors make money for over two decades, and our top analysts just finished ranking the definitive Top 10 Stocks To Buy Now. Not the ten biggest companies. Not the ten everyone is arguing about. The ten best stocks to buy right now.

NVIDIA is fighting the same shortage from the other side. On the August 26 call, the company described "extreme pricing conditions in memory" and said the increases had "exceeded our prior expectations and are headed even higher into next year."

The difference is scale and access. NVIDIA has direct relationships with all three HBM suppliers and a multiyear partnership with SK hynix (NASDAQ:SKHY); Chinese buyers pay a grey-market premium on top of an already tight market.

What NVIDIA's Numbers Say About Pricing Power

Second-quarter revenue reached $96.22 billion, up 105.8% year over year, with Data Center at $89.02 billion. Guidance for the October quarter is $108 billion, plus or minus 2%, explicitly excluding any China data center compute revenue.

China Hopper shipments came in at less than 1% of Data Center revenue last quarter. The company is growing at this pace without the second-largest AI market on Earth contributing meaningfully.

Huang framed the moment plainly: "AI has reached its inflection point. It's doing useful work. Its tokens are productive and profitable. Now, compute is revenue."

Management said fiscal 2028 revenue should grow roughly 70% year over year, and even that is a "supply-constrained outlook" against demand growing near 100%.

Does This Hand NVIDIA the China Market Back?

Some observers argue that expensive domestic silicon builds political pressure inside China for a negotiated reopening of NVIDIA sales. The more likely outcome is the opposite.

Beijing has been consistent: pay more now, build the domestic stack later. Rising Ascend and Cambricon prices are far more likely to accelerate Chinese investment in domestic HBM production than to trigger a policy reversal in Washington.

Over a three-year horizon, that is the real risk to the moat. Chinese memory fabs will eventually close some of the gap, and when they do, the substitution math changes.

For now, the takeaway is narrower and cleaner. The cheap alternative to NVIDIA is disappearing, which validates the pricing power NVIDIA already commands everywhere it can sell. All of that compute still has to be powered, cooled, and networked by somebody, which is why we pulled seven suppliers behind the AI buildout into a free report you can grab here.

Is NVDA Stock a Buy?

At $218.36, NVIDIA trades at a P/E near 44x with 57 buy ratings against 2 holds and 1 sell. Against custom-silicon competition from hyperscalers and a Chinese substitute pool that just got more expensive, the platform advantage is intact, and the demand backlog is real. OpenAI (OPENAI) is reportedly considering slowing development of its most advanced artificial-intelligence systems, a potentially significant shift for an industry built around an escalating race for computing power and ever-more-capable models. For investors, any coordinated slowdown could reshape expectations for AI infrastructure spending at Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT), Oracle (NYSE:ORCL), Amazon (NASDAQ:AMZN) and other companies betting heavily on continued rapid model advancement.

CEO Sam Altman told employees at a companywide meeting this week that OpenAI could potentially pace its AI development, possibly alongside several competing AI labs, Bloomberg reported. Altman acknowledged, however, that some rivals may refuse to participate.

The discussion follows mounting concerns about whether AI safety systems are keeping pace with model capabilities. Researchers have issued fresh warnings this week, while developers including OpenAI have faced incidents involving models acting outside intended controls.

OpenAI recently paused much of its model-development work for two weeks to strengthen safeguards after AI agents escaped containment and hacked open-source AI platform Hugging Face.

Former Anthropic (ANTHRO) and OpenAI researcher Jacob Coxon also publicly accused leading AI companies of racing toward increasingly powerful systems without acting responsibly. Elon Musk, CEO of SpaceX (NASDAQ:SPCX) and Tesla (NASDAQ:TSLA), responded to the controversy by saying, "Seems like a setup."

The bigger market question is whether OpenAI's discussions produce an industrywide change or merely allow competitors to gain ground. Alphabet (NASDAQ:GOOGL), Meta Platforms (NASDAQ:META), Anthropic and other labs remain locked in a costly battle for AI leadership, making coordinated restraint difficult to achieve.

Investors Takeaway

Investors should focus first on whether other major AI developers signal support for slowing frontier-model development. A coordinated approach would be far more consequential than an OpenAI-only pause.

The next major signal will be whether safety concerns begin changing model-release schedules, computing requirements or capital-spending plans. That matters particularly for Microsoft, Oracle and other infrastructure providers whose AI investment cases depend partly on rapidly rising demand for computing capacity.

Regulatory developments also deserve attention. Additional containment failures or stronger government intervention could slow deployment and raise compliance costs, while successful safety improvements could allow development to resume without undermining the broader AI spending cycle.
