text:
Dive Brief:

Kura Oncology is spinning out a new company that intends to develop medicines known as menin inhibitors on diabetes and other cardiometabolic diseases.

Called Caspian Therapeutics, the startup is initially focusing on a drug codenamed “KO-7246.” Preclinical testing has suggested the treatment might help the body regenerate pancreatic beta cells and produce more insulin in people with diabetes. That strategy represents a potentially new use for menin inhibitors, two of which have been approved in the U.S. to treat leukemia.

Caspian has raised $50 million in financing to get going. While far smaller than the $100 million-plus “megarounds” that have become commonplace in biotech, Caspian can get by with less because it shares operational teams with Kura, according to Kura CEO and Caspian executive chairman Troy Wilson. Kura participated in the funding and will retain about a 50% stake in the fledgling firm, which is also backed by BVF Partners, Eli Lilly, the T1D Fund and other investors.

Dive Insight:

Kura had already started testing menin inhibition outside of oncology before it decided to spin out Caspian. But it wasn’t until this past spring that Wilson and his team realized KO-7246 needed a separate home.

“As a company at our size and stage, you cannot be all things to all people,” Wilson said in an interview. “We needed to bring in dedicated expertise and capital. We needed to infuse it with the assets, the people and the capital to make a difference.”

Kura and another company, Syndax Pharmaceuticals, have already proven that blocking menin — a protein that controls gene expression and cell signaling — is an effective tool in treating acute myeloid leukemia. In AML, stifling an interaction between menin and another protein called KMT2A prevents leukemia cells from rapidly reproducing. Syndax’s therapy, Revuforj, was approved last October. Kura’s, called Komzifti and co-developed with Kyowa Kirin, got to market shortly afterwards. It generated nearly $15 million in sales in the first half of 2026.

In diabetes, blocking menin can “take the brakes off pancreatic beta islet cells,” which is necessary for restoring normal levels of glucose and insulin production, Wilson said. KO-7246 is being tested in both Type 1 and Type 2 diabetes.

Caspian has one direct competitor in Biomea Fusion, which is also making a menin inhibitor that’s currently in mid-stage testing. But while Biomea “has a time advantage,” Caspian’s drug could have a superior safety profile, Wilson said.

Importantly, preclinical research has shown Caspian’s drug doesn’t appear to spur abnormal growth in other cell types. Additional data will be presented at a medical meeting later this month. The company has not disclosed when it plans to begin human testing.

Caspian is also exploring the possibility of using menin inhibitors in conjunction with GLP-1 drugs to help patients who cannot control their diabetes with existing treatments.

“Once you have a drug that has good safety and clinical activity, give it to talented scientists and clinicians, and they’ll help you learn how to use it,” Wilson said.

Kura’s stock price dipped slightly on Wednesday morning, though TD Cowen analyst Phil Nadeau wrote in a note to clients that the spinout appeared to “offer shareholders opportunity for upside while reducing the downside risk.”

The deal enables the “efficient development of KO-7246 while Kura’s resources remain focused on oncology,” Nadeau wrote.

text:
Instacart has debuted Clementine, an artificial intelligence-powered grocery shopping assistant. Now available to customers across the US and Canada on the Instacart Marketplace, the new feature can transform a conversation, grocery list or recipe into a personalized shopping cart within seconds.

Clementine is built on more than 1.6 billion lifetime orders, a catalog of more than 2 billion items, and more than 10 million daily inventory signals from 100,000 stores across over 2,200 retail banners, according to the company.

"Every night, millions of families ask the same question: 'What's for dinner?' Not knowing the answer, let alone what to shop for, is one of the most universal human experiences, and a problem Instacart is built to solve," said Chris Rogers, CEO of Instacart. "We've spent nearly 15 years learning how families shop and eat, and Clementine puts that knowledge to work. It learns from the preferences you share and the way you've shopped on Instacart. It can help you stay on budget and surface what's actually in stock at your chosen store, handling enough of the weekly planning that the mental load actually feels lighter."

According to Harris Poll data cited by Instacart, more than 80% of Americans say figuring out what to make for dinner causes stress, and nearly a third claim the hardest part of dinner is deciding what to make. More than three in five said they would use an AI assistant for help.

Based on early results, orders placed with Clementine on average include more items than a typical basket and exceed Instacart’s $115 average basket size, according to the company.

"Grocery shopping is one of the most routine things people do, and also one of the most personal," said John Adams, vice president and head of product at Instacart. "What we built with Clementine is a system that understands both of those things — not just what you need, but how you eat, what you love, and what's on the shelves at your store right now. Whatever you're craving or planning for, Clementine can get you there. The more you use it, the more it feels like a natural part of how your household shops, becoming something you reach for week after week."

The introduction of Clementine builds on Instacart’s AI strategy, which includes Cart Assistant, an enterprise AI shopping assistant developed for retailers’ owned and operated websites and apps. Grocery partners using Cart Assistant include Food Bazaar, Heritage Grocers Group and Woodman’s, with ALDI US, Harmon’s, The Save Mart Companies, Stew Leonard’s and others to follow, per Instacart.

"AI is transforming how customers shop, and it's important for us to make sure our banners are at the forefront of that shift," said Adam Salgado, chief experience officer at Heritage Grocers Group. "Cart Assistant has made it possible to deploy AI technology quickly and in a way that feels authentic and personalized to each of our brands. For us, that includes the ability for our Spanish-speaking customers to use this technology, too, because a personalized experience means meeting people in the language they're most comfortable using."

This story was originally published on Grocery Dive. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily Grocery Dive newsletter.

Dive Brief:

Albertsons announced Wednesday that it has named Meg Whitman to the newly created role of executive chair of the company's board of directors.

Albertsons' chair, Kim Fennebresque, transitioned to lead independent director upon Whitman's appointment, and the company's board expanded from 10 to 11 members.

Whitman's appointment comes just a few months after Albertsons started a broad restructuring plan in response to disappointing first-quarter results in July.

Dive Insight:

In addition to her board responsibilities, Whitman will serve as an operations and strategic advisor to CEO Susan Morris as Albertsons works to sharpen its strategy and increase profitable growth. The announcement noted that Whitman's experience will be particularly helpful as Morris continues to streamline the company's operating structure around artificial intelligence technologies and a more consistent customer experience online and in stores.

Whitman's board member position took effect Tuesday, per an Albertsons Securities and Exchange Commission filing. Her term will expire at the company's 2027 annual meeting of stockholders or until a successor is elected.

Whitman brings more than 40 years of experience to Albertsons, including serving as president and CEO of eBay for a decade and as CEO of Quibi, a Los Angeles-based entertainment startup. Whitman also served as CEO of Hewlett Packard Enterprise, and as president, CEO and chair of Hewlett-Packard Company, according to the press release.

She currently serves on the corporate boards of AI cloud-computing company CoreWeave, fleet management company Motive Technologies and geothermal energy company Fervo Energy.

Outside of the business world, Whitman served as United States Ambassador to Kenya from 2022 to 2024 and was the Republican Party's nominee for California governor in 2010, the announcement noted.

"At this pivotal moment, I'm thrilled Meg is joining our board as Executive Chair," Morris said in a statement. "As we focus on moving faster and competing more effectively, Meg's strategic judgment, operating discipline and technology expertise will be invaluable. I look forward to partnering closely in the months and years ahead."

Whitman's appointment comes at a trying time for Albertsons. The company reported negative comparable-store sales growth and flat overall sales during its most recent quarter, and it has lowered expectations for its financial performance for the rest of fiscal 2026. In response to these lackluster results, Albertsons announced in July a new regional operating model that consolidates 11 divisions into four regions and unveiled plans to centralize its center store merchandising. At the time, Albertsons also announced that President and CFO Sharon McCollam plans to retire later this year and then serve in an advisory role with the grocer until its fiscal year ends in February.

description:
Discover how Accor supports women in building successful hospitality careers, developing new skills and progressing into leadership positions.
At Accor, supporting women means creating an inclusive workplace where people can grow at every stage of their careers.

text:
Discover how Accor supports women in building successful hospitality careers, developing new skills and progressing into leadership positions.

Behind every memorable hospitality experience are talented people who bring their expertise, creativity, and leadership to work each day. Women play an important role across the hospitality industry, from hotel operations and guest services to technology, finance, commercial teams and senior leadership.

But building a successful career is about more than getting your first job. It’s about having opportunities to learn, develop your skills, move into new roles and take on greater responsibility as your career evolves.

At Accor, supporting women means creating an inclusive workplace where people can grow at every stage of their careers. Through learning, mentoring, career mobility and leadership development, Accor aims to help its talent build careers with room to grow.

How does Accor support women in their careers?

Career journeys rarely follow a straight line. Someone might start in a first hospitality role, move into a management position, switch departments or eventually take on a leadership role.

That’s why career development matters at every stage.

Accor is committed to fostering an inclusive workplace where women have access to opportunities to learn, develop and progress. This includes learning opportunities, mentoring initiatives and leadership development programs designed to help people build the skills and confidence they need for their next career step.

The aim is simple: create an environment where people can explore their potential and shape a career that works for them.

Building a career in hospitality: Growth starts from day one

You don’t need to know exactly where your career will take you when you start working in hospitality.

One of the benefits of a hospitality career is the variety of roles, teams and experiences available. A first role can lead to opportunities in another department, a different hotel, a new country or a leadership position further down the line.

For women starting their careers in hospitality, access to development opportunities can help turn that potential into progress.

Learning on the job, building new skills and connecting with experienced colleagues can all help employees understand what they’re capable of and where they want to go next.

From learning new skills to taking the next step

Career development doesn’t stop once you’ve secured your first role.

As careers progress, employees may want to develop specialist expertise, move into management or explore a completely different area of the business. Supporting that progression means making opportunities to learn and develop accessible throughout an employee’s journey.

Accor’s approach to talent development includes opportunities to build skills, explore career mobility and prepare for greater responsibility.

That could mean moving from an operational role into management, developing expertise in a corporate function or taking on responsibilities across a wider team.

For women looking to progress their careers, these opportunities can help make the next step feel achievable.

Why is women’s leadership important in hospitality?

Women’s representation in leadership continues to be an important conversation across the hospitality industry and beyond.

Diverse leadership teams bring different experiences and perspectives to decision-making. They can challenge assumptions, encourage new ideas and help create workplace cultures where more people can see themselves progressing.

Accor continues to work towards increasing opportunities for women to grow into management and leadership positions across its global network.

Leadership development is about more than reaching a particular job title. It’s about developing the confidence, experience and skills to manage people, make decisions and influence the direction of a team or business.

For women considering their next career move, hospitality can offer multiple opportunities to develop those skills.

Learning from women across Accor

One of the advantages of working for a global hospitality company is the opportunity to learn from colleagues with different backgrounds, experiences and perspectives.

Across Accor, women contribute to many different areas of the business, from hotel operations and commercial teams to technology, finance and executive leadership.

Their career stories show that there isn’t one definition of a successful hospitality career.

Someone might discover a passion for leading a hotel team. Another might build a career in finance, technology or marketing. Others may move between countries, brands or departments as they develop their experience.

These different career journeys can provide inspiration for women considering what their own next step could look like.

Creating opportunities for women to grow and lead

Supporting women at every career stage is about creating the conditions for people to develop their skills, pursue their ambitions and take on new challenges.

For Accor, that means continuing to invest in empowering and developing diverse talent across its global network.

It also means recognising that career development looks different for everyone. Progress could mean becoming a team leader, moving into a specialist role, changing departments, working internationally or taking on a senior leadership position.

The important thing is having the opportunity to keep moving forward.

What can a career in hospitality offer women?

A career in hospitality can offer far more variety than many people expect. With opportunities across hotels, corporate functions and specialist teams, there are multiple ways to build experience and develop a career.

For women at different stages of their professional journeys, that could mean:

Starting out: gaining practical experience, building confidence and discovering where your interests lie.

Developing: learning new skills, taking on greater responsibility and exploring career mobility.

Moving into management: building leadership skills and learning how to support and develop a team.

Growing as a leader: taking on broader strategic responsibilities and helping shape the future of hospitality.

Your career doesn’t have to follow a set path. The next opportunity might take you somewhere you didn’t expect.

Ready to take the next step in your hospitality career?

Women are shaping the future of hospitality every day as Heartists®, managers, specialists and leaders across Accor.

With opportunities to learn, develop and explore different career paths, hospitality can be a place to build a career that evolves alongside your ambitions.

ExxonMobil NYSE: XOM Chief Financial Officer Neil Hansen said the company is relying on technology, project execution and operational performance to support long-term shareholder returns as energy markets navigate supply disruptions and higher refining margins.

Speaking at the Barclays Energy-Power Conference, Hansen said the company’s strategy is designed to operate across commodity-price cycles and changing energy systems. He cited ExxonMobil’s ability to execute major projects at lower cost and faster speed than competitors, as well as its efforts to centralize operating organizations across the enterprise.

Striking Oil: How the U.S. Play for Venezuela Fuels Supermajors

“We want to be defined by what we do well, not necessarily by the products that we produce,” Hansen said.

Supply disruption shifts pressure toward refining

Addressing the Middle East supply disruption and conditions surrounding the Strait of Hormuz, Hansen said the situation underscored the importance of affordable and reliable energy. He said market mechanisms have largely responded as expected, including releases from commercial and strategic inventories, higher supply from countries including the United States and Brazil, and demand destruction in chemicals and refining.

The 2026 Blueprint: 6 Stocks for a Brand New Portfolio

For the most part, oil prices have settled into a relatively range-bound environment, he said. However, ExxonMobil sees refining as the current pinch point in the energy system.

Hansen attributed higher refining margins partly to products not leaving the Middle East and reduced availability of crude needed by Asian refineries. He also cited developments involving Ukraine and Russia, as well as lower Chinese product exports.

He said ExxonMobil’s integrated model helps the company capture value as it moves among stages of the value chain. The company has organized itself around value chains spanning feedstocks, manufacturing, logistics and end consumers, while centralizing functions including supply chain, trading, technology, operations and project execution.

Hansen pointed to the company’s ability to qualify alternative crude supplies for Asian refining and chemical facilities during disruptions around the Strait of Hormuz as an example of how those capabilities can support operations.

Permian synergies exceed initial expectations

Hansen said ExxonMobil’s acquisition of Pioneer Natural Resources has performed better than anticipated. The company initially expected to generate about $2 billion annually in synergies from the transaction, but has doubled that amount, according to Hansen.

He described the integration as a “best of both” approach, combining ExxonMobil’s technology and operating capabilities with practices it adopted from Pioneer. The company remains focused on raising recovery rates in the Permian Basin, where Hansen said only a relatively small portion of the resource in the ground is currently recovered.

ExxonMobil is advancing 40 complementary technologies intended to improve primary and secondary recovery and enhance capital efficiency, he said. Some of the technologies could produce equivalent volumes with fewer wells. Hansen reiterated the company’s objective of doubling recovery in the Permian and said its outlook for the asset remains optimistic.

On future acquisitions, Hansen said ExxonMobil can remain selective. The company will seek transactions where it can apply its capabilities to create substantially more value than the current owner, rather than pursuing deals simply to add volumes or assets.

LNG growth and Guyana cash flow

Hansen said ExxonMobil continues to view the long-term fundamentals for liquefied natural gas as sound. While the company had expected near-term market length entering the year, he said Middle East developments have pushed that expectation out.

The company’s priority in LNG is to bring on advantaged, low-cost supply that can generate high returns, rather than to pursue geographic diversification for its own sake, he said. ExxonMobil’s portfolio includes operations and projects in the Middle East, Papua New Guinea, Mozambique and the U.S. Gulf Coast through Golden Pass.

Hansen also said ExxonMobil recently announced plans with Total in Papua New Guinea under which ExxonMobil will take operatorship and increase its equity interest.

In Guyana, Hansen said the company reached the “desaturation” of its cost bank faster than expected—about two years earlier, even after accounting for oil-price effects. He said the milestone reflects project execution and the performance of existing floating production, storage and offloading vessels.

ExxonMobil has recovered approximately $55 billion of costs in Guyana, Hansen said. While the development is expected to result in slightly lower entitled volumes—estimated at about 100,000 barrels per day beginning in the third quarter—he said it is expected to double free cash flow between 2025 and 2030.

The company’s fifth Guyana FPSO is already in the water, and ExxonMobil is working to advance a ninth vessel, he said. Hansen added that quicker cost recovery will increase receipts for the Guyanese government.

Focus extends beyond 2030

Hansen said ExxonMobil has growing confidence in its plan to add $25 billion in earnings and $35 billion in cash flow through 2030, with earnings growth moving closer to $30 billion. He said the company is also pursuing opportunities beyond that period, including LNG projects, frontier exploration, undeveloped discovered resources, Proxxima resins and graphite for batteries.

In Proxxima, Hansen said the company has demonstrated value in uses such as lighter rebar and coatings requiring fewer applications. ExxonMobil has made a final investment decision on a blend plant intended to produce up to 120,000 KTA of resins, he said. In graphite, the company is working with original equipment manufacturers to demonstrate faster battery charging, more capacity and longer duration.

Hansen said future structural savings are expected to come increasingly from ExxonMobil’s centralized organizational model and a new enterprise-wide system, rather than primarily from divestments.

text:
AXA has entered into a partnership with US technology company Publicis Sapient to support the next phase of its AI transformation.

The French insurer said the arrangement centres on the continued buildout of its Global AI Hub, which is designed to scale AI agents across the group's operations.

Publicis Sapient supplies enterprise AI platforms and services.

AXA Group operations CEO, group chief technology & AI officer Matthieu Caillat said: "As we continue to scale AI across the Group, our priority is to combine safe and efficient AI, strong governance and practical business applications that create lasting value."

AXA said the hub provides shared, global and standardised foundations for AI agents, with the goal of reducing time-to-market and costs, freeing AXA entities to focus on business value rather than building common AI infrastructure independently of one another.

"The collaboration combines AXA's unique insurance, AI and responsible AI expertise with the specialist AI talent and engineering solutions of Publicis Sapient, a technology company that provides enterprise AI platforms and services," AXA said in its statement.

The insurer said the first version of the Group-wide, vendor-agnostic hub was rolled out in July and is currently in use across five AXA entities.

It is intended to serve as a "secure" base for implementing, governing and operating AI capabilities, while supporting technology independence and building in compliance, FinOps, governance, human oversight, SafetyOps and security at every stage of the AI life cycle.

"It also enhances the ability to allocate and orchestrate specific capabilities and LLMs [large language models] across use cases in a strategic and cost-effective manner," it added.

AXA units in Germany, France, Switzerland, the UK and AXA XL are currently developing use cases spanning motor claims automation, customer email processing and enterprise knowledge management.

Publicis Sapient EMEA & APAC financial services head David Murphy added: "We are excited to partner with AXA to establish the enterprise AI capabilities, engineering approaches and the necessary governance to accelerate AI adoption securely and consistently across the Group in support of AXA's long-term AI ambitions."

The partnership follows AXA XL's agreement last month to acquire the remaining shares in S-RM, taking full ownership of the UK-based corporate intelligence and cybersecurity consultancy.

S-RM, founded in 2005, serves clients across more than 140 countries and operates nine international offices spanning six continents.

text:
Key Takeaways

The FDA has accepted and filed Nanoscope Therapeutics’ BLA for Mogenry, an investigational optogenetic gene therapy for patients with RP and severe vision loss

The application is supported by phase 1/2a and phase 2b/3 data, with RESTORE meeting its primary and key secondary endpoints and showing visual acuity improvements at weeks 52 and 76

If approved, Mogenry could become the first gene-agnostic therapy to improve vision in patients with RP and severe vision loss, with a one-time, in-office administration approach that does not require genetic testing

The FDA has accepted and filed Nanoscope Therapeutics’ biologics license application (BLA) for Mogenry (sonpiretigene isteparvovec; MCO-010), an investigational optogenetic gene therapy designed to restore vision in patients with retinitis pigmentosa (RP) and severe vision loss.

The regulatory milestone moves the one-time therapy into FDA review. If approved, Mogenry would become the first gene-agnostic therapy to improve vision in patients with RP and severe vision loss, according to Nanoscope.

"FDA acceptance and filing of our BLA for MOGENRY is a crucial milestone that brings us a critical step closer to offering a one-time, in-office treatment option to the retinitis pigmentosa community with severe vision loss, who have no approved therapy today," said Sulagna Bhattacharya, Chief Executive Officer of Nanoscope Therapeutics. "The strength of our RESTORE data, together with the durability we have observed through long-term follow-up in the REMAIN study, give us confidence in MOGENRY's potential to become a new standard of care for patients living with RP having severe vision loss. We look forward to working closely with the FDA throughout its review."

The FDA has issued a PDUFA (Prescription Drug User Fee Act) date in the first half of 2027. Nanoscope told Eyewire News it is actively preparing to be commercial-ready in the first half of 2027.

The application is supported by efficacy and safety findings from a Phase 1/2a study (NCT04919473) and the phase 2b/3 RESTORE trial (NCT04945772). RESTORE was a multicenter, randomized, double-masked, sham-controlled clinical trial evaluating Mogenry in patients with RP and severe vision loss. According to Nanoscope, the trial met its primary and key secondary endpoints, demonstrating improvements in visual acuity at weeks 52 and 76.

The investigational therapy was also reported to be well tolerated, with no treatment-related serious adverse events.

Most patients treated in RESTORE subsequently continued into the REMAIN study, which is providing long-term follow-up data included in the BLA.

Allen C. Ho, MD, professor of ophthalmology at Thomas Jefferson University, director of retina research at Wills Eye Hospital, and chief medical advisor for Nanoscope Therapeutics, said the therapy’s potential accessibility could be particularly important for patients outside major academic centers.

“Mogenry does not require genetic testing or administration in a surgical suite, which could enable broad adoption by community retina practices,” Dr. Ho said in the company’s announcement.

Mogenry is designed to address vision loss through optogenetics rather than targeting a particular disease-causing mutation. The approach is intended for patients who have experienced photoreceptor loss from retinal degeneration. That distinction could potentially broaden the population eligible for treatment compared with mutation-specific gene therapies because patients would not need to have a particular genetic variant to qualify.

Nanoscope is also positioning the therapy as a one-time, in-office treatment, potentially avoiding the surgical-suite administration required for some ocular gene therapies.

text:
Kura Oncology has spun out a biotech armed with $50 million in fresh funding to take forward a next-generation diabetes treatment.

The new entity, named Caspian Therapeutics, will be focused on KO-7246, a highly selective menin inhibitor that Kura has billed as being “purpose-designed for chronic metabolic diseases.”

To fund KO-7246 through preclinical development and into a first-in-human study, Kura has secured $50 million in funding. The financing round was led by BVF Partners and included Eli Lilly—a major player in the diabetes space—alongside the diabetes-focused venture philanthropy fund T1D Fund, Invus, Montanova, members of Kura’s leadership team and “several successful biotech entrepreneurs,” according to a Sept. 9 release.

A portion of the funding has also been earmarked to support development of another menin inhibitor aimed at diabetes and other cardiometabolic diseases.

Kura will own half of Caspian and the biopharma has supplied the spinout with the relevant “intellectual property and know-how” to make KO-7246 a success. Kura has been busy rolling out Komzifti in the U.S. this year after securing FDA approval for the menin inhibitor to treat acute myeloid leukemia at the tail end of 2025.

That approval came just weeks after Syndax Pharmaceuticals secured the first-ever approval for a menin inhibitor in the form of its own leukemia therapy Revuforj.

So far, menin inhibitors have been used to block the interaction between the menin protein and specific mutant proteins that drive aggressive forms of leukemia. However, Kura has been exploring the ability of menin to selectively stimulate pancreatic β-cells to increase insulin production.

“Our preclinical findings have strengthened our conviction that menin inhibition has the potential to address the underlying loss of functional β-cell capacity, rather than simply managing its consequences,” Kura’s Chief Scientific Officer Francis Burrows, Ph.D., said in the release.

“The consistency of the findings across Type 1 and Type 2 diabetes models, together with their translation into human islet systems, provides a strong rationale to advance KO-7246 into clinical development,” Burrows added.

Kura is planning to unveil the preclinical data to back up this thesis at the European Association for the Study of Diabetes Annual Meeting in Milan, Italy at the end of the month.

“Menin inhibition is a core area of Kura’s scientific and drug-development expertise, and the emerging biology in diabetes represents an exciting opportunity to extend that expertise beyond oncology,” Kura CEO Troy Wilson, Ph.D., added in this morning’s release.

“By establishing Caspian with dedicated leadership and external capital, Caspian can pursue the potential of KO-7246 while Kura remains focused on executing its oncology strategy,” explained Wilson, who will take up the role of executive chairman of the spinout’s board of directors.

title: U.S. Bank's Stablecoin Pilot on Stellar Sends a Clear Signal: Banks Want Their Own Rails
description:
U.S. Bank completed a live cross-border payment using its proprietary USBDC stablecoin on the Stellar network on September 9, 2026, exactly seven days before the scheduled mainnet launch of Circle Arc.
Rather than joining an open institutional platform, U.S. Bank is prioritizing the development of its own proprietary infrastructure.
Gunjan Kedia, Chairman and CEO of U.S. Bank, framed the development as a tactical advancement: "This live pilot demonstrates our ability to accelerate global cash management and money movement capabilities."
This shift reflects a broader trend in institutional blockchain adoption, where firms are increasingly comfortable operating outside of traditional regulatory consensus.
In the high-stakes game of institutional money movement, the winner will be the one that balances the speed of the blockchain with the ironclad security of the vault.
text:
U.S. Bank completed a live cross-border payment using its proprietary USBDC stablecoin on the Stellar network on September 9, 2026, exactly seven days before the scheduled mainnet launch of Circle Arc. According to recent reporting, while the industry prepares for the debut of the platform designed to integrate traditional financial institutions, the fifth-largest U.S. bank is notably absent from the list of Circle Arc's 12 founding validators.

The timing suggests a deliberate strategic pivot. Rather than joining an open institutional platform, U.S. Bank is prioritizing the development of its own proprietary infrastructure. The pilot, conducted between internal entities in North America and Europe, was not customer-facing but served as a rigorous stress test for the bank's internally developed Digital Asset Platform. The bank validated essential functions including minting, redemption, freezing, and clawback capabilities-the unglamorous mechanics required to bridge public blockchain technology with the rigid demands of bank-grade compliance and risk management.

Gunjan Kedia, Chairman and CEO of U.S. Bank, framed the development as a tactical advancement: "This live pilot demonstrates our ability to accelerate global cash management and money movement capabilities." Jamie Walker, Head of Digital Assets and Money Movement at U.S. Bank, echoed this sentiment while emphasizing the bank's conservative approach to innovation: "This pilot is another step forward in our broader digital asset strategy. Our focus remains on delivering solutions that solve real client challenges while maintaining the safety, security and reliability that clients expect from U.S. Bank."

Despite the corporate momentum, the bank remains cautious. There is no commercial rollout timeline, and specific details regarding transaction corridors and volumes remain undisclosed. This pilot highlights the three distinct models currently vying for dominance in the institutional space: the bank-proprietary model exemplified by U.S. Bank's solo run on Stellar; the open institutional model represented by Circle Arc, which seeks to standardize the tokenization of bank deposits; and the consortium model, where a 21-bank group is working toward its own dollar token slated for the first half of 2027.

These competing visions for the future of settlement economics are not merely technical differences. As explored in our coverage of capital flows in agentic AI, the question for institutional allocators and fintech builders is which rail will ultimately absorb the market. If a bank can successfully internalize its cross-border treasury operations, liquidity management, and collateral movement, it may find little incentive to join a broader, shared network that requires ceding control or sharing fees. This shift reflects a broader trend in institutional blockchain adoption, where firms are increasingly comfortable operating outside of traditional regulatory consensus.

However, we must remain grounded in the reality of the current stage. This is a pilot, not a production launch. The industry is littered with the ghosts of ambitious blockchain experiments that never made it past the internal testing phase. U.S. Bank has proven it can move money on a blockchain, but proving it can do so at scale, across diverse regulatory jurisdictions, and with the reliability of a legacy settlement system is an entirely different challenge.

For now, the bank is playing a long game, building on the foundation of its November 2025 announcement with the Stellar Development Foundation. Whether this proprietary rail becomes the standard or merely a bespoke solution for internal efficiency remains to be seen. In the high-stakes game of institutional money movement, the winner will be the one that balances the speed of the blockchain with the ironclad security of the vault.

text:
Contents

Adobe is expanding its PDF service around the Acrobat software family into a platform for AI-powered document work. The new AI functions are intended to summarize content from files and prepare it as interactive reports, overview slides, or audio formats. According to the manufacturer, tools for companies will make knowledge from large document collections accessible or automatically evaluate contract data.

At the core of this is the “Adobe Productivity Agent,” according to Adobe. It is intended to consolidate information from PDF documents and other connected data sources.

AI Creates Audio Summaries and Infographics

In the future, Acrobat will be able to convert extensive text documents into interactive reports with diagrams, images, and navigation. The AI will first ask for the desired outcome and then prepare the results as a visual summary. This could allow for a quick overview of quarterly figures, personnel statistics, or market analyses without having to read long texts.

Another innovation is audio formats. Users can load the content of PDF documents or web links into a workspace and simply have it read aloud or have an audio summary or a personal podcast format generated from it. This is intended to help prepare for meetings on the go or consume content away from the screen.

Graphically Prepare Resumes, Invoices, and Reports

The “Stylize” function is intended to allow documents to be designed in a simple way: Using templates from Adobe Express, it transforms resumes, invoices, reports, and offers into an appealing layout. The AI is intended to adapt the existing content to the chosen template without changing the source text.

Student Spaces: Online Tool for Students

Student Spaces, which were launched as a test in April 2026, are now available worldwide. Students can create flashcards, quiz questions, study aids, and summaries from uploaded documents there. The platform digitizes handwritten notes and supports with resumes and preparation for job interviews.

AI for Businesses: Knowledge Base from PDF Documents

Customers of Acrobat Studio for Enterprise can use the “Knowledge Base” tool to convert document collections into a searchable knowledge base. According to Adobe, it supports Office files, web pages, text files, and emails in addition to PDFs. It can automatically synchronize documents from SharePoint and Google Drive. Employees should be able to ask questions in natural language and receive answers that are directly linked to the respective text passages in the original sources.

The “Analyzer” tool is intended to convert information from thousands of similar business documents into structured data. Its use is conceivable for contracts, service descriptions, invoices, or audit reports. For example, finance, purchasing, and IT departments could extract terms, termination clauses, reporting obligations, or data security requirements from many documents. Here too, the results should contain references to the respective source.

Adobe itself uses Analyzer, according to its statements, to check customer contracts for unusual clauses. Furthermore, the system is intended to detect discrepancies between contract data and entries in the customer management system.

Security and Control

Adobe assures that customer documents will not be used to train its own generative AI models. For large organizations, Adobe offers role-based access, logs, and other management functions. According to Adobe, Knowledge Base and Analyzer are built on the infrastructure of Acrobat Sign and the company’s own framework for security and compliance.

Pricing and Availability

According to Adobe, the audio and visualization functions are included in the plans for Acrobat Studio, Adobe Express, and Acrobat AI Assistant Plus. Acrobat Studio costs 29.99 euros per month. Knowledge Base, Analyzer, and the new audio and visual functions are available in Acrobat Studio for businesses. Adobe did not disclose prices in this category.

text:
Today Adobe is executing a major architectural shift for its Acrobat platform by rolling out a suite of AI capabilities designed to transform the 30-year-old document format from a passive reading medium into an interactive workspace.

Powered by a new underlying Productivity Agent, the updated Acrobat automatically parses unstructured PDF data into a variety of outputs. Instead of manually reading dense documents, users can now command the system to generate audio podcasts, synthesize visual report decks via Adobe Express templates or auto-format raw text into corporate branded layouts.

The major update reflects Adobe's effort to keep its core PDF format—which sees over 400 billion documents opened annually—relevant as generative AI changes how we interact with software. Instead of keeping workflows locked inside the Acrobat app, Adobe is extending these agent capabilities natively into third-party ecosystems, including ChatGPT, Claude, WhatsApp, Chrome and Edge.

Kowledge Base And Analyszer

For organizational workflows, the platform is introducing two major ways to ingest data. Knowledge Base connects directly to cloud storage services like SharePoint and Google Drive, indexing document archives so teams can run natural-language queries across thousands of different PDFs, Microsoft Office files and emails simultaneously.

The new Analyzer tool in Acrobat can extract tabular and structured insights from unstructured contracts, statements of work and vendor agreements. It can automatically flag SLAs, auto-renewal dates and inflation adjustments across large document portfolios.

"Acrobat is already where millions of people come to read their most important information, and now it's where people can understand it faster and more comprehensively," says Abhigyan Modi, Senior VP of Adobe's Productivity Product Group.

Adobe is also scaling its education footprint following the global rollout of Student Spaces. The AI tool for students is designed to convert lecture notes and textbooks into interactive flashcards, practice quizzes and source-cited study guides.

Pricing and Availability:

The new audio, visual and enterprise tools are available across Adobe's Acrobat Studio, Express and AI Assistant Plus tiers, with advanced cross-repository analytics reserved for enterprise accounts. Detailed pricing varies by market.

text:
Just under a year after netting its first US approval for a cancer-fighting menin inhibitor, Kura Oncology is launching another firm to apply the same idea to diabetes.

Kura has created Caspian Therapeutics to develop small-molecule menin inhibitors for diabetes and cardiovascular diseases. Formally launching today, Caspian has $50 million to get its drug candidates off the ground. Backers include the T1D Fund and Eli Lilly and Company, alongside a spate of firms that had previously invested in Kura. Kura owns about 50% of Caspian.

Kura CEO Troy Wilson calls menin the “Swiss army knife of targets.” It’s an epigenetic modifier that controls gene expression by modulating the methylation patterns on DNA. In certain forms of acute myeloid leukemia—the disease that Kura’s menin inhibitor Komzifti, or ziftomenib, was approved to treat last year—menin interacts inappropriately with KMT2A fusion proteins, driving the cancer. Komzifti stops menin and the fusion proteins from interacting.

In diabetes, Wilson says, menin represses proteins involved in controlling the cycle of β cells within the islets of Langerhans in the pancreas cells. So a menin inhibitor could selectively expand the mass of β cells in people with diabetes, increasing insulin production.

“People are trying to chisel away at diabetes, both type 1 and type 2, in lots of different ways,” Wilson says. “They’re doing cell therapy. They’re doing implants. They’re doing a whole bunch of approaches of autoimmunity, GLP-1s. There is no other therapeutic target that selectively regrows the pancreatic β islet cells. It just doesn’t exist. So this thing is kind of a unicorn.”

The teams at Kura and Caspian expect to begin a Phase 1 clinical trial of Caspian’s lead compound, the small-molecule menin inhibitor KO-7246, by the end of next year and have data from that study in 2028. Caspian will present more information about KO-7246’s chemical properties at the annual meeting of the European Association for the Study of Diabetes, which will begin in Milan later this month.

For Wilson, Caspian is the ninth company he’s started. Its name, Caspian, refers to the Caspian Sea, into which the Kura River drains.

Caspian itself has only one full-time employee: Rob Spencer, who’s acting as president and chief operating officer. Caspian and Kura will functionally partner on a lot of the drug-development process. The start-up will also work with Lilly’s contract research organization Lilly ExploR&D. “There's no point, right now, in building a lot of redundant capability,” Wilson says.

Boston Scientific (BSX) stock dropped after the company said it can no longer stand behind its Q3 and full-year 2026 sales and profit forecasts.

A cybersecurity incident first identified on August 25 was the culprit. Unauthorized activity on some of the company’s IT systems caused a network outage that disrupted manufacturing, as well as the processing and shipping of customer orders.

Boston Scientific recently guided for full-year 2026 adjusted earnings between $3.28 and $3.32 per share, with sales growth of 5.5% to 6.5%.

Sterilization facilities are back online, and manufacturing has resumed across most global facilities.

The company said the incident’s effects were limited to select internal infrastructure, and product quality checks found no problems beyond disruptions to new activations on its cardiac device remote-monitoring platform.

Stifel analyst Rick Wise said investors are increasingly viewing 2026 as a “lost year” for the company and are shifting their focus to what 2027 might look like instead.

J.P. Morgan analyst Robbie Marcus added that the cyberattack makes it harder for investors to judge the company’s underlying business trends, delaying any read on growth and competitive dynamics in key areas like electrophysiology and its Watchman heart device.

This isn’t happening in isolation either.

Boston Scientific is just the latest healthcare company to get hit by a cyberattack, following similar incidents at Abbott Laboratories, Stryker, Medtronic, and Novo Nordisk.

Healthcare and medical device companies have clearly become frequent targets recently.

What the Market Is Telling Us About Boston Scientific Stock

The stock’s 6% drop suggests the market isn’t panicking but it is worried for sure, but there’s real uncertainty baked into that reaction.

Boston Scientific stock was already under pressure heading into this news, since the company trimmed its 2026 profit forecast in July because of softer demand for its Watchman device.

Now, with operational guidance pulled entirely, investors are left waiting for clearer answers.

Boston Scientific plans to give an updated outlook when it reports Q3 results on October 28.

Until then, Boston Scientific stock will likely stay sensitive to any headlines about recovery progress, since the company has said the full financial impact of the cyberattack remains unclear.

For now, the market seems to be treating this as a temporary operational setback rather than a deeper business problem, but that view could shift once actual numbers come in next month.

text:
Block is applying to the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency to form Builders Bank & Trust, N.A., an uninsured national trust bank under its jurisdiction that would focus on digital asset custody and fiduciary services. Approval would bring parts of Block’s bitcoin, stablecoin and other digital asset-related businesses under direct federal oversight.

It would not be a traditional commercial bank. According to Block, Builders Bank would not take in customer deposits or make loans to customers. Instead, its mandate would be custody and other fiduciary functions for assets like Bitcoin and stablecoins, using its national charter to provide regulatory uniformity as those services expanded.

Submission of an application does not authorize the bank to open, as Builders Bank cannot open for business until the proposal has been through the OCC’s review process, the OCC has issued its approval, and the bank has met any organizational requirements, as well as any conditions imposed, e.g., governance, capital, compliance, operational readiness.

Lee Woolley, currently Block’s Digital Asset Strategy Lead, is expected to serve as Builders Bank’s president and CEO. Woolley has been in the financial industry for more than 20 years, including as head of the Treasury Department Federal Credit Union. He also held senior positions at Northern Trust and BNY Mellon.

Block already has U.S. banking activity via Square Financial Services, an industrial bank licensed in 2021, although Builders Bank would be a standalone federally supervised bank focused on trust and custody activities.

Read More: Bitcoin Just Hit a Critical $80K Level. What Happens Next Could Decide September

The application comes as crypto and fintech firms have increasingly sought national bank and trust charters from the OCC, which maintains a list of pending licensing applications from companies wanting to offer digital asset products or services.

Corporate Applications Search allows the public to search applications, status, and regulatory actions. When considering a national bank charter application, the OCC’s chartering process involves financial, supervisory, and legal analyzes.

As applied to digital asset applicants, a federal charter would subject approved trust activities to a single national framework, but would not convert a non-deposit-taking trust company into a retail depository institution and would not confer deposit insurance.

Other large digital asset firms, including Ripple, Circle, Paxos, BitGo and Fidelity Digital Assets, received conditional approvals from the OCC in late 2025, with additional applicants entering the process through 2026.

Later, Circle would receive final approval to form a federally regulated national trust bank, a form of regulation above and beyond being a conditionally chartered bank.

Block’s application is currently pending before the OCC, which can ask for more information, approve the application, impose conditions, or reject the application. The institution cannot begin operations as a national trust bank unless and until the regulator grants the charter and Builders Bank meets the requirements to commence banking operations.

Rating agencies Moody's and S&P assigned investment-grade ratings to Sun Pharmaceutical Industries-India's largest pharmaceutical company-over the proposed 11.75-billion dollar acquisition of US-based Organon & Co. S&P Global Ratings assigned a preliminary 'BBB+' long-term issuer credit rating, while Moody's Ratings assigned a 'Baa1' long-term issuer rating to the pharmaceutical major. Both agencies have maintained a 'stable' outlook for the company. Baa1 and BBB+ are investment-grade credit ratings that indicate adequate payment capacity with moderate credit risk. The rating actions follow Sun Pharma's binding bid in April 2026 to acquire a 100 percent stake in Organon for an enterprise value of 11.75 billion dollars. The transaction is expected to close by March 2027 following/subject to regulatory approvals.

According to S&P, the acquisition will bolster Sun Pharma's business position, almost doubling its revenue base to about Rs 1.3 trillion (around 14 billion dollars) by FY28. Organon is expected to contribute 40-45 percent of the group's EBITDA post-acquisition. "The Organon acquisition will materially strengthen Sun Pharma's scale, geographic reach and growth platforms in women's health and biosimilars," said Kaustubh Chaubal, Senior Vice President at Moody's Ratings. "The acquisition will bolster Sun Pharmaceutical's business position... we estimate Sun Pharmaceutical's revenue will increase to about Rs 1.3 trillion (about 14 billion dollars) in fiscal 2028, from our estimate of Rs 645 billion (about 7 billion dollars) in fiscal 2027 (ex-Organon)," S&P said in a release.

"Organon's presence in markets such as China and Korea offer Sun Pharma an opportunity to cross-sell its products; it currently has limited presence in the two countries," S&P stated. Moody's noted that Sun Pharma had secured 12 billion dollar committed acquisition bridge loan from a syndicate of global banks. As of March 31, 2026, the company held cash balances of approximately 3.6 billion dollars. Analysts believe Organon will strengthen Sun Pharma’s scale, reach, growth and diversification.

Lilly’s acquisition strategy starts long before an acquisition The deals Lilly announced in 2026 are the most visible expression of its strategy, but the process often begins earlier.
text:
A year ago, Eli Lilly’s pipeline strategy appeared relatively straightforward, with Mounjaro and Zepbound generating an increasingly large pool of cash, and Lilly using it to build beyond diabetes and obesity. Acquisitions in radiopharmaceuticals, inflammatory bowel disease, precision oncology and cardiovascular gene editing suggested a company deliberately turning the incretin boom into a broader pipeline.

Since then, Lilly has kept that momentum going and at a greater pace. In 2026 alone, it completed acquisitions spanning in vivo cell therapy, hematology and sleep medicine, including Orna Therapeutics, Kelonia Therapeutics, Ajax Therapeutics and Centessa Pharmaceuticals. It then acquired three companies to establish an infectious disease portfolio and agreed to buy AtaiBeckley, adding a pipeline of experimental neuropsychiatric drugs.

But the Eli Lilly pipeline has also become more dependent on the franchise funding all of this expansion. In the second quarter of 2026, the company generated $23.0 billion in revenue. Mounjaro contributed $9.9 billion and Zepbound another $4.9 billion, meaning the two tirzepatide brands alone accounted for nearly two-thirds of Lilly’s sales.

But its newer immunology, oncology, and neuroscience products are themselves growing quickly: Lilly reported 121% year-on-year growth across those key products in Q2. However, its incretin business is expanding from an entirely different base.

The incretin franchise is becoming a portfolio of its own

A year ago, Mounjaro and Zepbound were the commercial engine in Eli Lilly’s pipeline, while orforglipron and retatrutide were the most important candidates waiting behind them. Since then, that pipeline has started to look less like a succession plan and more like an attempt to occupy different parts of an expanding cardiometabolic market.

Lilly said the growth of its incretin franchise was primarily volume-driven: Mounjaro demand remained strong despite lower realized prices, while Zepbound also grew despite lower prices, including previously announced reductions for cash-paying patients. Across Lilly as a whole, sales volume rose 60% in the quarter while realized prices fell 13%.

And the reach of tirzepatide, the active ingredient behind the two blockbuster drugs, has continued to expand too. in August, the FDA approved tirzepatide to reduce the risk of major cardiovascular events in adults with type 2 diabetes at high cardiovascular risk.

What has changed most clearly is what sits around tirzepatide. In last year’s article, orforglipron was still a phase 3 oral GLP-1 candidate, notable partly because it could offer an easier-to-use alternative to injectable incretins. It is now a marketed product. The FDA approved the drug as Foundayo in April 2026 for adults with obesity or overweight and weight-related comorbidities.

Lilly is already trying to broaden Foundayo beyond obesity, and its type 2 diabetes program has produced positive phase 3 results across several settings. In ACHIEVE-3, Lilly reported that the highest dose produced greater reductions in both A1C and body weight than oral semaglutide 14 mg, while ACHIEVE-2 and ACHIEVE-5 also met their primary endpoints. The company submitted orforglipron for type 2 diabetes in the U.S. during the second quarter of 2026.

Retatrutide is also moving forward. In the phase 3 TRIUMPH-1 trial, participants receiving 12 mg lost an average of 28.3% of body weight after 80 weeks; among participants with a baseline BMI (body mass index) of at least 35 who continued into an extension, average weight loss reached 30.3% at 104 weeks.

The phase 3 program also shows why Lilly sees retatrutide as more than another obesity drug. TRIUMPH-1 also evaluated obesity-related knee osteoarthritis and obstructive sleep apnea, with Lilly reporting reductions in knee pain and apnea-hypopnea events alongside weight loss.

Two further pivotal trials reported in July extended that picture. In TRIUMPH-2, people with obesity or overweight and type 2 diabetes lost an average of up to 20.8% of their body weight at 80 weeks. In TRIUMPH-3, which enrolled people with severe obesity and established cardiovascular disease, weight loss reached 22.6%. Lilly says the five positive phase 3 trials now provide the clinical package needed to pursue registrations in obesity, obstructive sleep apnea and knee osteoarthritis pain, with a U.S. filing planned for the first quarter of 2027.

These drugs address different parts of the market: Tirzepatide provides the established injectable backbone; Foundayo offers a convenient oral option that could broaden access and primary-care use; and retatrutide is being developed around very high weight-loss efficacy and obesity-related complications.

The company is trying to make metabolic medicine larger than tirzepatide itself. If Foundayo expands the addressable population while retatrutide raises the efficacy ceiling and extends treatment further into conditions such as sleep apnea and osteoarthritis, Lilly could end up with several complementary products and the largest cardiometabolic franchise.

The diversification bets are starting to produce evidence

The diversification bets Lilly made in 2024 and 2025 are still too early to judge by commercial impact, but several have moved far enough to take another look. That is particularly true for Verve Therapeutics, which we described as a long-horizon cardiovascular gamble last year: a one-time gene-editing treatment for high cholesterol was compelling in principle, but questions around delivery, durability, and safety remained.

There is now early human evidence backing that bet. In phase 1b, a single infusion of VERVE-102 produced reductions in circulating PCSK9 of between 51% and 88%, with LDL cholesterol falling by as much as 62% at the highest dose. Lilly reported that the reductions were sustained during follow-up extending to 18 months and plans to begin enrolling a phase 2 study by the end of 2026. However, this was an interim analysis in just 35 participants, so it does not yet establish the long-term safety or clinical benefit.

The picture is similar, but still preliminary, in inflammatory bowel disease. Lilly bought Morphic for $3.2 billion largely around MORF-057, an oral α4β7 integrin inhibitor intended to complement its existing Omvoh franchise. A phase 2a study in 35 patients with moderately to severely active ulcerative colitis found that MORF-057 was generally well tolerated and improved histological and other disease measures. The larger phase 2b trial remains active but is no longer recruiting. Lilly’s existing inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) backbone has continued to progress too. Among Omvoh-treated patients who had achieved disease clearance after one year, 63.5% maintained it after four years in the LUCENT-3 extension study.

On the oncology front, when Lilly agreed to acquire Scorpion Therapeutics’ PI3Kα program in 2025, STX-478 was still being tested in an early-stage trial, and the appeal was its ability to selectively inhibit mutant PI3Kα while sparing the wild-type protein, potentially avoiding some of the toxicity that has constrained the class. The drug, now called tersolisib, has since entered phase 3 in first-line HR-positive, HER2-negative advanced breast cancer with PIK3CA mutations. The study is still recruiting patients and is testing tersolisib alongside endocrine therapy and a CDK4/6 inhibitor.

With the radiopharmaceuticals bets, the story is less straightforward. POINT Biopharma was one of Lilly’s most important diversification moves, bringing both radioligand programs and manufacturing capabilities into the company. Its lead PSMA-targeted asset met the primary endpoint of the phase 3 SPLASH trial – median radiographic progression-free survival was 9.5 months versus 6.0 months with an androgen-receptor pathway inhibitor, corresponding to a 29% reduction in the risk of progression or death. But interim overall survival was immature and unconvincing.

More importantly, the commercial rights had already been licensed to Lantheus before Lilly acquired POINT. By late 2025, after the SPLASH trial reached its prespecified overall-survival event target, Lantheus said the results remained heavily confounded by crossover and that it did not currently plan to pursue an NDA or invest further in PNT2002. The trial itself remains active for follow-up, with POINT, now a Lilly subsidiary, still listed as sponsor.

Verve has generated early human proof-of-concept, Morphic remains promising but unvalidated, and Scorpion’s lead asset has advanced into phase 3, while POINT’s most advanced radioligand has encountered a much less straightforward path. The bets Lilly made in 2024 and 2025 are beginning to generate evidence, but most are still years away from showing the benefits Lilly expects.

Eli Lilly is buying optionality

The acquisitions announced in 2026 look broad; Lilly is acquiring technologies that give it several possible routes into new modalities or therapeutic areas.

In February, Lilly agreed to acquire Orna Therapeutics for up to $2.4 billion. Orna combines engineered circular RNA with lipid nanoparticles to program cells inside the body. Its lead candidate, ORN-252, is a clinical trial-ready CD19-directed in vivo CAR-T for B-cell-driven autoimmune diseases, but Lilly explicitly framed the acquisition more broadly, as a platform for genetic medicine and in vivo cell engineering.

Two months later, Lilly agreed to spend considerably more on a different solution to essentially the same technological problem. Kelonia Therapeutics, acquired for $3.25 billion upfront and up to $7 billion including milestones, uses engineered lentiviral particles to deliver genetic cargo selectively to T cells in the body. Its most advanced program, KLN-1010, is a BCMA-directed in vivo CAR-T already in phase 1 for relapsed or refractory multiple myeloma. Whereas Orna relies on circular RNA and lipid nanoparticles, Kelonia’s platform is designed to integrate the CAR construct into T cells using targeted lentiviral delivery.

Lilly also paid about $6.3 billion upfront for Centessa Pharmaceuticals, with another $1.5 billion potentially payable through contingent value rights. The immediate attraction is cleminorexton, an orexin-2 receptor agonist that has reached phase 2 development in narcolepsy and idiopathic hypersomnia. But Centessa also brings additional OX2R agonists, giving Lilly the foundation for a new sleep-wake disorder franchise within neuroscience.

Another important move was the acquisition of Ajax for up to $2.3 billion, gaining AJ1-11095, a type 2 JAK2 inhibitor for myelofibrosis and polycythemia vera. Early phase 1 data reported in June showed signs of clinical activity, although the program remains at an early stage. Lilly was already a founding strategic investor in the company before agreeing to buy it. Lilly can gain exposure to emerging science through investment, follow its development, and potentially bring the company completely in-house if the program matures.

Then, just over a week ago, Lilly agreed to acquire Merida Biosciences for up to $2.875 billion, adding an antibody-engineering platform designed to selectively remove disease-causing autoantibodies. Its lead candidate, MER511, is already in phase 1 development for Graves’ disease and thyroid eye disease. The acquisition adds yet another technological approach to Lilly’s expanding immunology pipeline.

Lilly’s expansion has also reached therapeutic areas where it previously had little presence. In May, it announced three acquisitions simultaneously: Curevo, LimmaTech Biologics and Vaccine Company, deals worth up to $1.5 billion, $780 million and $1.55 billion respectively. Curevo brings an experimental shingles vaccine designed to improve tolerability; LimmaTech is developing vaccines against bacterial pathogens including Staphylococcus aureus, Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis; and Vaccine Company has a nanoparticle platform with an Epstein-Barr virus vaccine as its lead program. Lilly described the transactions as an expansion into infectious disease built around prevention and differentiated technology platforms.

Lilly has also poured cash into neuroscience. In July, Lilly agreed to acquire AtaiBeckley for approximately $2.8 billion upfront and up to $1 billion more in contingent payments. AtaiBeckley is developing neuroplastogens, led by BPL-003, an intranasal formulation of mebufotenin for treatment-resistant depression. The deal also includes VLS-01 and earlier-stage compounds, extending Lilly from neurodegenerative disease and sleep medicine into experimental treatments for psychiatric disorders.

Lilly has enough financial capacity that it does not need to identify a single therapeutic area or technology as the obvious successor to metabolic disease. It can own several possible futures at once, sometimes acquiring an entire new franchise, sometimes buying a platform applicable across diseases, and in the case of in vivo CAR-T, even acquiring different technological routes toward the same broad objective.

Lilly’s acquisition strategy starts long before an acquisition

The deals Lilly announced in 2026 are the most visible expression of its strategy, but the process often begins earlier. Ajax Therapeutics is a good example, as Lilly was a founding partner before the final acquisition.

Lilly’s Catalyze360 initiative is specifically built to engage early-stage biotechs and is agnostic of therapeutic area. Its four components cover different needs: Lilly Ventures provides investment capital; Gateway Labs provides laboratory space and scientific engagement; ExploR&D offers drug-development support from discovery through clinical proof of concept; and TuneLab gives participating companies access to AI and machine-learning models trained on Lilly’s proprietary drug-discovery data.

Lilly said at the beginning of 2026 that Catalyze360 had supported more than 180 biotech companies since 2023. Its Gateway Labs innovation hubs alone have hosted companies that raised more than $2 billion and advanced more than 50 therapeutic programs since 2019. Not all of those companies are Lilly investments, much less potential acquisition targets.

This early-stage ecosystem is clearly distinct from Lilly’s corporate business-development operation. Catalyze360 is designed to engage companies at early stages across therapeutic areas. The program is not a formal conveyor belt from startup to acquisition, but it gives Lilly several different points of contact with external innovation.

The more immediate strategic advantage may simply be access. Lilly can invest in young companies without having to acquire them, provide infrastructure to others without investing at all, and reserve larger commitments for technologies that mature into partnerships or acquisition opportunities. Ajax shows that those stages can connect, but Lilly does not need every relationship to end in ownership for the network to be useful.

A year ago, the company could reasonably be described as using the proceeds of its incretin franchise to make targeted bets beyond diabetes and obesity. Since then, those earlier bets have begun producing clinical evidence, Lilly has spent billions acquiring additional technologies and therapeutic pipelines, and its infrastructure for finding external innovation has expanded to reach hundreds of biotechs.

Yet Lilly remains highly dependent on incretins, with Mounjaro and Zepbound now accounting for nearly two-thirds of quarterly revenue. At the same time, Foundayo and potentially retatrutide could broaden the metabolic franchise even further.

text:
At present, international beauty giants are scrambling to enter the Indian market, with L'Oréal and Estée Lauder making successive layouts, and another acquisition has now been finalized.

On September 7, FSN E-Commerce Ventures, the parent company of Indian beauty e-commerce giant Nykaa, announced that it has completed the acquisition of an additional 24.2% stake in the clean beauty brand Earth Rhythm, with a maximum consideration of 94 million rupees (about 6.6571 million RMB).

△ Source: Global Cosmetics News

Three additional investments in four years

The connection between Nykaa and Earth Rhythm dates back to 2022. At that time, Nykaa acquired an 18.51% stake in Earth Rhythm for 416 million rupees (about 29.57 million RMB).

In August 2024, the Nykaa board of directors approved an additional investment plan of up to 4.45 billion rupees (about 316 million RMB), intending to bring the brand into its subsidiary system through a combination of primary and secondary transactions. In November of the same year, the first round of additional investment was implemented, with Nykaa investing 3.95 billion rupees (about 280 million RMB), raising its shareholding ratio to 74.63%.

In June 2025, Nykaa completed the second round of capital injection, investing another 500 million rupees (about 35.5 million RMB), further increasing its shareholding ratio to 75.8%.

This time, Nykaa acquired an additional 24.2% stake in Earth Rhythm for 94 million rupees (about 6.67 million RMB), raising its shareholding ratio from 75.83% to 100%.

So far, Nykaa has invested a total of about 956 million rupees (about 67.84 million RMB) in four years, completing the wholly-owned acquisition of Earth Rhythm.

The acquired Earth Rhythm was founded in 2015, initially starting as a home workshop under the name Soapworks India, and renamed Earth Rhythm in 2019. The brand is positioned as a clean beauty brand, and all its products are claimed to be vegan, cruelty-free, biodegradable, and free of artificial fragrances. Currently, its products cover skincare, hair care, makeup and body care, with bestsellers including the Ultra Defence Hybrid sunscreen and dual-purpose lip and cheek makeup.

△ Source: Earth Rhythm official website

According to the exchange disclosure document filed by Nykaa in May 2026, Earth Rhythm achieved a turnover of 237 million rupees (about 16.86 million RMB) in the 2025-2026 fiscal year, which is lower than 267 million rupees (about 18.96 million RMB) in the 2024-2025 fiscal year and 324 million rupees (about 23 million RMB) in the 2023-2024 fiscal year, showing a year-on-year declining trend.

This acquisition is part of Nykaa's "House of Nykaa" strategic layout. Since Nykaa launched its first own makeup brand Nykaa Cosmetics in 2017, it has gradually built its own brand matrix. Up to now, Nykaa has built nine brands on its own, covering multiple categories such as makeup, skincare, bath & body, perfume, Indian apparel, Western apparel, underwear and sportswear [1].

Moreover, Nykaa has made frequent moves in brand acquisitions in the past two years.

In August 2024, it increased its stake in skincare brand Dot & Key from 51% to 90% for 2.653 billion rupees (about 188 million RMB); in August 2025, it acquired the remaining 40% stake in healthy snack brand Nudge Wellness for 1.5 million rupees (about 106,500 RMB) to achieve full holding; in September 2026, it completed the final equity acquisition of clean skincare brand Earth Rhythm for 94 million rupees (about 6.674 million RMB).

In addition, in August 2026, the Nykaa board of directors also approved the acquisition of a 51% stake in high-end skincare brand Aminu for up to 320 million rupees (about 22.72 million RMB), and the transaction is still in progress.

There are also reports that Nykaa is in talks to acquire a majority stake in 82°E, a skincare brand founded by Bollywood star Deepika Padukone. If the deal is reached, it will further enrich Nykaa's brand matrix in the high-end skincare sector [2].

Multinational giants are collectively scrambling to enter the Indian beauty market?

Nykaa's successive moves are only a slice of the Indian beauty capital boom.

From the time dimension of 2025 to the present, multinational giants are accelerating their entry into this country, which L'Oréal calls "one of the fastest growing beauty markets in the world", through the path of investment and acquisition [3].

As can be seen from the figure above, L'Oréal has successively bet on two major brands: efficacy skincare brand Deconstruct and tech skincare brand Innovist; Unilever took the acquisition of 90.5% stake in UprisingScience, the parent company of Minimalist, through its Indian subsidiary as a starting point, and successively invested in five brands through its venture capital department within 15 months: luxury Ayurveda brand Ras Luxury Skincare, customized beauty brand Skin-inspired, clean beauty brand indé wild, niche skincare brand Secret Alchemist, and clay mask specialist brand ClayCo; Estée Lauder has achieved 100% holding of high-end Ayurveda skincare brand Forest Essentials; Kose has also taken a 10% stake in efficacy skincare brand Foxtale.

This acquisition boom has also spread to local Indian giants, from FMCG groups to retail giants, who have joined the battle one after another.

In November 2025, Indian beauty and personal care company Honasa Consumer invested 10 million rupees (about 710,000 RMB) in oral care brand Fang to obtain a 25% stake; in March 2026, Indian retail giant Reliance Retail acquired clean skincare brand Pahadi Local; in April, Reliance Retail took over Anomaly, a vegan hair care brand founded by Bollywood star Priyanka Chopra Jonas; in August, another Indian FMCG giant Wipro Consumer Care acquired scientific skincare brand Dermatouch for 38.75 billion rupees (about 2.75 billion RMB).....

Nykaa's completion of the final equity acquisition of Earth Rhythm has temporarily drawn a full stop to its four-year-long investment layout. However, Earth Rhythm's revenue has declined for two consecutive years.

Against the backdrop of multinational giants such as L'Oréal and Unilever, as well as local forces such as Reliance Retail, flocking into the Indian beauty track, how Nykaa, as a "cross-border player", can truly transform its brand matrix into performance growth in the Indian beauty market surrounded by giants, remains an open question. This "battle of the gods" in the Indian beauty industry has only just entered a white-hot stage.

Note: All foreign currency amounts mentioned above are converted at the exchange rate on September 8, 2026, 1 rupee ≈ 0.071 RMB, 1 US dollar ≈ 6.71 RMB.

Information Sources:

[1] Reported by Indian media Mint on June 9, 2025;

[2] Reported by The Economic Times on April 6, 2026;

[3] ANI. India is country of opportunities, fastest beauty products market in world: L'Oreal chief, 2025-06-02.
